projects.title: How much outer step does overlapping communication with compute cost, and how many rounds should be in flight?
projects.summary: Applying the averaged displacement τ rounds late obeys zτ+1 − zτ + c = 0 with c = αs, so the stable step is exactly c < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1): 2, 1, 0.62, 0.45 for τ = 0…3, shrinking like 1/τ. The fastest single-mode rate is the double root τ/(τ+1), and the stationary noise floor is an exact Yule–Walker solve (closed form (1+c)/((1−c)c(2+c)) at τ = 1) that matches literal delayed-DiLoCo simulation to 0.3%. Delay is free at small steps (+1% at α = 10−3, τ = 4) but multiplies the floor by 3.9× at c = 0.8. At an equal floor each delay round costs only about 6% more rounds, so the wall-clock-optimal delay is exactly ⌈latency / compute time⌉ (1.9–7.5× faster than no overlap). Stylised: constant delay, identical workers, quadratics, no momentum.

projects.title: Does error feedback rescue the noise floor that compressed local SGD loses?
projects.summary: Workers keep the unsent part of their displacement and add it to the next message. On a quadratic with random sparsification the second moments close exactly: stability requires αs < 2(2−ρ)Nρ/(Nρ2+4(1−ρ)) — half the unbiased limit for a single worker, above the uncompressed limit for large cohorts — and the floor has a closed form that returns to the uncompressed one at small steps (1.08× at ρ=¼ where unbiased compression pays 4×) while the mean keeps its speed. What the residual buys is unbiasedness: dropping converges to the send-rate-weighted mean, feedback to the true mean, but at a variance that only pays off for very small steps. Top-k is simulation only; stylised quadratics.

projects.title: How should a server weight workers that ran different numbers of inner steps?
projects.summary: With worker i running Hi steps, weighted averaging has exact floor α2Σwi2Vi/(r(2−r)), r = αΣwisi. One worker's information is I∞tanh(λH/2): H=8 carries 20% of the ceiling and H=64 93%, so a fast device is worth far less than its step count. Information-optimal weights span at most 2×, hence equal weights lose at most 9/8 (measured ≤1.09), whereas step-proportional (FedAvg-style) weights lose up to 1.76× per mode and 10.5× on three modes when one worker in eight is 256× faster. Matched to simulation within 1%. Stylised: quadratic, shared optimum (no client drift), fixed Hi.

projects.title: What does a median or trimmed-mean outer step cost local SGD, and what does it buy against Byzantine workers?
projects.summary: Because the median and trimmed mean commute with shifts, the outer loop stays exactly linear: floor αVwv/(s(2−αs)) plus a bias Vwm2/s2, with the same stability limit as averaging. With no attackers the median costs N·Var = 1.35 to 1.56 (→ π/2). With a fraction ε of attackers its bias is bounded (Φ(z) = 1/(2(1−ε)): 0.18 noise-sigmas at ε = 1/8) and beats averaging once the attack offset exceeds about 1.4 sigmas; more workers shrink only the variance part (total loss 0.103 → 0.102 from N=8 to 128), while a longer inner loop shrinks the bias (39× from H=1 to 256). Trimming exactly the attacker count is worse than the median. Matched to simulation within 1.3%. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared curvature, constant-offset attackers.

themes.name: Digital twins & sim-to-real
themes.blurb: What a simulated clone of a physical system is worth for training and validating controllers: transfer regret, validation, and randomization.

projects.title: A stereo twin that adds Gaussian noise to depth gets the median right: what does it get wrong about over-range errors, safety margins and averaging compared with real disparity-space noise?
projects.summary: Real sensor: disparity noise σ = 0.25 px on a 700 px, 0.12 m rig (matches only above 1 px, so 84 m), depth = reciprocal of disparity; twin: Gaussian depth noise with the linearised sd. The median is exact, but the (gated) mean is biased by about s2 (+1.5% at 40 m) and over-estimates of distance are far more common than the twin says: at 40 m P(depth > 1.5Z) is 0.0026 vs 10−5 (191×), and a twin mean + 3σ margin is exceeded 10× as often as designed. Matching the variance leaves 41× on that tail. Averaging 1024 frames of depth floors at 1.5% error where the twin predicts 0.4%, whereas averaging disparity converges; at 60 m the range floor loses 5.5% of looks and flips or removes these effects (reported as a negative result). Stylised: Gaussian i.i.d. disparity noise, no outliers or calibration error.

projects.title: A rigid-body twin of a cart carrying liquid predicts no slosh: how wrong is that, what does a slosh-safe move cost, and what does a stale frequency calibration do to it?
projects.summary: Real cart: 80 kg body with a damped spring-mass slosh mode (20 kg liquid, 0.5 Hz at full fill); twin: one rigid mass. The twin gets the centre of mass exactly (RK4 error ~10−14 m) but predicts zero slosh; for a bang-bang rest-to-rest move the real residual is 4μa0sin2(ωT/4)/ω2, matched by exact propagation and RK4. The twin’s minimum-time move (3 m, 4.90 s) leaves 10.7 cm of slosh, 10× a 1 cm tolerance; the fastest move meeting it takes 7.60 s (55% slower) because zero-residual times are whole multiples of two slosh periods. Calibrating ω at a full tank is harmless down to half fill (−5% frequency, 9.5 mm) but at 25% fill the smallest safe null-tuned move takes 28 s vs 8.7 s recalibrated, worse than the tuning-free bound 24.7 s; at fixed acceleration the first unsafe null order is exactly ⌊asin(√ρ)/(π|ε|)⌋+1. Stylised: one linear slosh mode, bang-bang force, no shaper optimisation, no nonlinear slosh.

projects.title: Can an input shaper make a liquid-carrying cart’s move robust to a stale slosh-frequency calibration, and how fast can it be?
projects.summary: Follow-up to slosh-twin. Convolving the twin’s bang-bang acceleration with a ZV or ZVD shaper multiplies the undamped residual exactly by V(ε) = |sin(πε/2)| or sin2(πε/2), ε the frequency error (verified against exact propagation to 10 digits), while distance and the acceleration cap are preserved. Designed at a full tank, both shapers keep the 1 cm tolerance at every fill from 100% to 10% (ε down to −9.5%; worst residual 4.8 mm ZV, 0.6 mm ZVD) in 5.90 s and 6.90 s, where the null-tuned move needs 8 s at half fill and 28 s at 25% and below. Closed forms give the largest tolerated |ε| (e.g. 10.7% for ZV at half fill). Searching the design frequency for a fill band [0.1, 1] yields a 5.85 s ZV move, but only by detuning to spend the whole tolerance (worst residual 9.88 mm, no margin). Stylised: one linear slosh mode, ideal actuator, no nonlinear slosh.

projects.title: What is a digital twin worth for training a controller?
projects.summary: In a scalar linear-quadratic plant the twin-trained gain has exact deployment regret, asymmetric with a stability cliff: underestimating actuation to 0.21× is infinitely costly while 2× over costs 0.22. A twin can score perfectly on passive logs (log-score gap exactly 0) yet mistrain the controller, and closed-loop logs are blind along Δa = kΔb, so validation needs designed probing. Used as a ridge prior, a twin with bias δ is worth exactly σ2/(vδ2) real probe steps at every accuracy target (22 steps at δ=0.3), and removes small-sample divergence (3.1% to 0 at n=10). Matched to simulation within 1–4%. Stylised.

projects.title: How wide should domain randomization be, and what does it buy?
projects.summary: Randomizing the twin's input gain over ±ε trains a more conservative gain (monotone in ε; small-width law kε−k* = −(εb)2Jkbb/(6Jkk)) at a quartic price when the twin was right, and moves the deployment stability cliff out by about 15%. At 2.3× the twin's gain the nominal controller has regret 84 versus 1.4 at ε=0.9. But uniform-average training is not minimax: its worst-case regret exceeds the nominal gain's for ε ≤ 0.7, and the best width equals the prior's half-width, paying off only when the prior reaches the cliff. Stylised.

projects.title: What does it cost to keep a digital twin in sync with a drifting plant, and is probing worth it?
projects.summary: A Kalman twin tracks a drifting actuator gain from the closed-loop data the controller already produces. Its steady-state predictive variance is a closed-form quadratic root (m = q/2 + √(q2/4 + qσ2/v) for a random walk), matching closed-loop simulation to 1–3%, and control regret is ½Jkk(dk*/db)2m (0.00447 predicted vs 0.00466 simulated). A calibrate-and-freeze twin loses half its edge over the population mean after ln 2/(2(1−ρ)) = 34.5 steps. For one drifting parameter a dedicated probing budget never pays (information price 0.70 vs marginal value ≤ 0.04); for two, the closed-loop blind direction makes a fixed-gain twin unobservable and the mean-field optimal dither scales exactly as q1/6, yet simulation shows the controller’s own gain jitter supplies most of that excitation, so the mean-field law is an upper bound. Stylised.

projects.title: How often, and how long, should a digital twin be re-identified as the plant drifts?
projects.summary: For a twin refitted from dedicated experiments rather than filtered from operating data, the second-order-optimal schedule is closed-form: interval T* = (4cσ2/(vρqd2))1/3, with experiment downtime, estimation noise and drift regret exactly equal at the optimum, so excess cost scales as qd1/3 (fitted slope 0.333) and 10× cheaper experiments lower it only 2.2×. Misjudging the drift rate by 4× costs at most 26%. But the second-order optimum is unsafe: 0.7–15% of its cycles destabilise the loop, and a schedule with failure probability ≤ 10−3 costs 1.2–16× more and is 37–200× worse than an always-on Kalman twin. Stylised.

projects.title: What should you pay a digital-twin provider for?
projects.summary: A provider paid Brier score on the twin’s parameter reports its posterior mean; one paid the deployed control cost reports the Bayes gain, which is more conservative (0.778 vs 0.823 at posterior sd 0.3, mean 1) and equals domain randomization under the provider’s own uncertainty. Certainty equivalence costs a quartic in spread (16× per doubling); reports with equal squared error have regret ratios of 1.3–24×; a payment cap makes the elicited gain jump at a closed-form threshold M* (19.3 in the example) that decides whether rare catastrophic plants are priced in; and Brier under- or over-pays probing by a 15× spread in decision value per unit variance. Stylised.

projects.title: How long can a digital twin be wrong before you can prove it, and what does waiting cost?
projects.summary: A Gaussian-mixture e-process on the closed-loop residual audits a deployed twin continuously: it false-alarms 2.4% of the time against 58% for a z-test checked every step. Detection delay follows ≈ 2[ln(1/α)+½ln(1+τ2nU)]/(Δ2U) with U the controller’s own excitation (simulation 0–18% earlier); expected regret accumulated before detection is nearly independent of the gap (8–10 while per-step regret spans 38×); an expensive-control operator needs 11× longer to catch the same gap; and added probing pays only for gross errors (true gain above 2.25× or below 0.35× the twin’s), with the rule failing at the near-cliff edge. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a Gaussian-clutter radar simulator do to a CFAR detector's false-alarm rate?
projects.summary: A CA-CFAR threshold set in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured (K-distributed) clutter has an exact false-alarm law, matched to direct simulation to ~1%. At design 10<sup>−4</sup> the real rate is 9× (ν=5) to 30× (ν=2) too high, and 50× to 358× at 10<sup>−6</sup>; restoring it costs 1.9–3.7 dB of threshold at 10<sup>−4</sup>. If texture is shared across the window CFAR is unaffected, so the twin must model spatial correlation. A moment fit of ν from 1000 real clutter cells brings the median to 1.1× (90th percentile 2×), versus ~10<sup>6</sup> cells to threshold empirically. Stylised: no target, no measured data.

projects.title: Does a more robust CFAR detector survive a Gaussian-clutter radar simulator?
projects.summary: Four window detectors (cell-averaging, order-statistic at ranks 3N/4 and N/2, log-t) are calibrated in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter. None is meaningfully more robust: at design 1e−4 the false-alarm inflation is 30–44× at ν=2 and 8–9× at ν=5, and the ranking flips with ν and design rate. A known-scale oracle with no window noise inflates 2.88× at 1e−2, ν=2 against cell-averaging’s 3.02×, so most of the error is the test cell’s own texture, which reference cells cannot see. After repairing each threshold to the design rate, cell-averaging detects best everywhere (Rayleigh target, 20 dB, ν=2: 0.758 vs 0.744, 0.732, 0.703), and the twin’s promised detection probability is overstated (0.70 vs 0.43 at 15 dB). No interfering targets, so order-statistic detectors are tested away from their home ground. Stylised.

projects.title: What does a light-tailed simulated human do to a collaborative robot's timeout?
projects.summary: A robot that waits for a human and aborts after τ has cost J(τ) = wE[min(T,τ)] + cP(T>τ), with slope S(τ)(w − c·h(τ)). Simulated humans with constant or increasing hazard (exponential, Weibull) therefore have only corner-optimal timeouts and, when aborting costs more than the mean wait, never give up. Against a lognormal human (σ=1.2, an assumed model) the interior optimum is 9.4 s and the light-tailed twin’s regret is 3.7% of the optimum, rising to 37% (σ=1.6) and 81% (σ=2) for heavier tails and cheap aborts. A lognormal twin with the right mean and σ off by 0.2 recovers all but 0.5%. Fitting the correct family from n real trials costs regret ∝ 1/n, matched by the delta method to within 11% (0.0323 at n=10, 0.00034 at n=1000). Stylised: scalar i.i.d. response time, one fixed timeout, no real human data.

projects.title: What does a too-clean sensor twin do to a mapper's commit error?
projects.summary: A grid cell committed when log-odds built with a twin's sensor model reach ±A has, under the real sensor, an exact error set by the Lundberg exponent θ* (equal to 1 for a correct twin) with a rigorous optional-stopping sandwich. A twin whose free-space false-hit rate is 0.05 against a real 0.15 turns a 10−3 design into 1.45×10−2 (14.5×, matched by simulation; 260× at 0.30), and an optimistic occupied hit rate (0.8 vs 0.6) gives 26×. Committing at ln(1/ε)/θ* restores the target at 1.4–16× the latency, and the real-data estimate of θ* needs several hundred known-free observations before the tempered mapper stops exceeding target in over a quarter of maps. Stylised: one independent-beam cell.

projects.title: Does cloning an expert from logs recorded in a digital twin recover the expert?
projects.summary: Demonstrations logged as applied (actuator-clipped) actions bias a linear clone even in a perfect twin: at an actuator limit of 1 the clone gain is 0.58 against the expert’s 0.96 and its real cost is 9.8% higher, with the exact Gaussian-state gain k0 P(|k0x|<U) from Stein’s lemma. Twin errors act through the states they visit and can help: 0.25× noise cuts the gap to 0.002, 2× raises it to 0.75, and a loose twin limit of 3 nearly removes it. Log-state coverage narrower than half the saturation width recovers the expert, while DAgger with applied-action labels converges to a worse gain (0.5575, gap 0.169 vs 0.141). Stylised: scalar plant, population-level fit, no real logs.

projects.title: What does a too-clean digital twin do to a student cloned from a privileged teacher?
projects.summary: A teacher that sees the true state is trained in a twin and cloned into a student that sees only a noisy sensor. Least-squares cloning attenuates the gain to gP/(P+s), where P is the demonstration state variance, so the student depends on the twin only through its process-noise-to-sensor-noise ratio. A twin with a quarter of the real process noise yields a lazy student with excess cost 0.36 (s=0.5) to 1.11 (s=2) against 0.005 to 0.10 from an exact twin, 2.8–3.6× worse than on-policy DAgger in the same twin. On-policy imitation of an exact teacher is within 3.5% of the best memoryless student over 252 cases; cloning can cancel an actuator error, but the cancellation point moves with sensor noise. Injecting demonstration noise in the twin, set from one real scalar (Var z − s), recovers the on-policy gain in two rounds (regret 0.357 → 0.0035 → 0.00003). Stylised: scalar linear–quadratic, no robot data.

projects.title: What does a digital twin without sensor latency do to a tuned controller?
projects.summary: A scalar unstable plant is controlled by the LQR gain designed in a twin with no measurement delay. The exact stable-gain interval shrinks with the real delay (upper edge 1 at one step, 0.59 at two), so the twin-tuned gain (0.70) tolerates one step at 1.6× the delay-aware cost and is unstable from two; a retuned static gain costs 1.1–2.6× for delays 1–5, and a predictor built for the wrong delay is unstable in nearly every off-diagonal case tested. Identifying the delay from an i.i.d. probe takes about 2z2(1+1/snr) samples. Stylised: scalar plant, integer delay, known dynamics.

projects.title: When does a forecast-ensemble twin send the UAV to the wrong place, or make the update worse?
projects.summary: A UAV samples from a corridor to cut forecast error over a region it cannot enter, with sites and Kalman gain taken from a twin’s covariance; the real error after the update is exact (Joseph form, checked against simulation). A matched twin cuts the real error 22%; a twin whose correlation length is 2× too long claims −65% and delivers +28%, because updates are harmful beyond a closed-form radius (ln 2/(ℓr−2−ℓt−2))1/2. Amplitude errors are harmless for one observation but an under-confident twin double-counts over several. A finite ensemble drawn from the correct model already hurts: 10 members give +27% mean real error (71% of ensembles worse than no observation), 50 are safe, and localisation helps at small sizes but costs accuracy at large ones; fitting the length scale from real samples needs about 50. Stylised: 1-D Gaussian field, one static update.

projects.title: What does a deterministic-duration twin of a lab workcell promise, and how many stations does it buy?
projects.summary: A batch is split over k parallel stations with a serial arm handover; a twin running every step at its mean picks k = √(W/a) = 8 and promises 16 min. The real makespan uses the exact expected maximum of gamma branches (checked against harmonic numbers and simulation): with exponential branches it averages 1.86× the promise, only 2.6% of runs finish every branch within its mean, and the 95% quantile is 3.03× the promise. Whether the twin also buys the wrong layout depends on how variability scales with splitting: task-level variability makes it under-buy (optimum 12, 24.7% regret on the 95% quantile), while a chain of random unit steps cancels the effect so k = 8 stays optimal yet the real makespan is still 6–59% above the promise. Fitting the branch-time shape needs about 5 real durations to fix the decision and about 50 to make the predicted makespan accurate to 1%. Stylised: one fork-join stage, i.i.d. gamma branches.

projects.title: How firmly should a robot grip when its friction twin is too clean?
projects.summary: A pinch grasp slips if μF < w0 and crushes if F exceeds a fragility limit; with log-normal friction and crush force the expected loss is a sum of two normal CDFs in ln F and its optimum solves a quadratic. A twin whose friction spread is 0.1 instead of 0.3 grips softer, claims a risk of 1.1×10−5 and delivers 0.069 (4.0× the optimum; 11.6× at spread 0.05). A near-zero-spread twin has a flat zero-risk plateau, so its ‘optimal’ force is a tie-break: real slip 0.50 at the lower edge, 0.015 at the upper. Biased friction costs ≈ ½J″Δx² (85% of the optimum at −0.3 in log-friction), and a widened randomisation width can cancel a known bias but costs 1.5× the optimum if the bias is of opposite sign. A plug-in from n real friction measurements has regret matched by the delta method within 5% for n ≥ 50. Stylised: static friction threshold, chosen parameters, no contact dynamics or reactive re-grasp.

projects.title: How much battery should a UAV carry when its twin has a constant wind?
projects.summary: A leg flown at airspeed v against a headwind that is uniform across flights costs P(v)/(v−w) in energy per distance; a constant-wind twin has no spread. Its cruise speed is nearly right (1.100 vs the real optimum 1.123, regret 0.10%), but its energy claim is low by exactly artanh(x)/x with x = a/(v−μ) (3.5% here), and a battery sized to that claim runs out in 50% of real flights (42% with a 5% margin). A 5% depletion target needs a 39% margin and 1% needs 44%, in closed form, and the real-optimal speed trims only 39.2% to 37.6%. The speed error itself grows to 6.4% of the optimum at wind half-width 0.6, and the twin speed meets a stalling wind (infinite energy) once the half-width exceeds v−μ = 0.80. Refitting the twin to n = 50 logged winds beats the constant-wind speed in 97% of fits. Stylised: one leg, constant airspeed, wind fixed within a flight, chosen parameters, no gusts or turn-back.

projects.title: What does a too-clean odometry twin do to a SLAM loop-closure gate?
projects.summary: A back end accepts a loop closure when its squared residual is below a gate; true closures are N(0, s2I), aliased ones are wider, and the cost is a weighted sum of two chi-square probabilities with a closed-form optimal gate in 2-D. A twin whose odometry noise is half the real value picks a gate that claims a cost of 0.094 and 2.1% of true closures rejected; in reality it rejects 38.2% (checked against simulation), costs 4.4× the claim and has 62% regret; a conventional α = 1% gate rejects α1/ρ2 = 32%. A too-pessimistic twin (ρ = 0.5) is not safe either (145% regret), regret depends strongly on how costly a false closure is, a fixed inflation factor is a bet on the true noise, and re-fitting the variance from about 59 ground-truthed closures brings regret under 1% of the twin’s. Stylised: isotropic Gaussian 2-D residuals, hard gate, known costs, no real odometry data.

projects.title: What does an odometry twin that is too clean do to a loop-closure gate?
projects.summary: A scalar position filter is tuned in a twin with drift variance T and gates loop closures by a chi-square test on its own covariance. With every closure accepted the real posterior variance is exact (1.47×, 2.14×, 4.03× the twin’s claim for real/twin drift-sd ratios 1.5, 2, 3; simulation within 1%), and genuine closures fail the 99% design gate 5% of the time at ratio 2. With the gate on, rejection compounds into lock-out: real error is 9–16× the ungated value at ratio 2 and 56–182× at ratio 3, growing with horizon. The gate halves error against aliased closures when the twin is right (0.52 vs 1.27) but is 8× worse than no gate at ratio 2 (13.9 vs 1.72), and a gate retuned with the real drift beats no gate only up to ratio 2. Fitting drift from measured ground truth fixes the median by 10 cycles but the lock-out tail needs about 30 (28% of trials lock out at 3). Stylised: scalar error, Gaussian drift, simulated not measured.

projects.title: How often should a mapping team rendezvous when its twin's odometry drift has no bias?
projects.summary: Robots reset their dead-reckoning error at rendezvous; the real error variance is s2t + b2t2 (white noise plus a per-run bias rate), but a twin fitted on short-horizon increments sees only the first term, so it plans a rendezvous every 10 and claims a peak error std of 3.16. The real optimum solves a cubic; at a bias/noise ratio ρ = 0.1/0.3/1/3 the twin's interval has 0.19/1.35/8.65/34.6% regret, the real error is exactly √(1+ρ) times the claim, and under an error budget the twin breaches it for 8–55% of every cycle. In the pairwise frame used for map merging a shared bias cancels (twin regret 5.3% → 0.10% at bias correlation 0.9). Repair needs ground-truth error at a long lag as well as a short one and about 5–10 runs to beat the twin reliably. Variance law and pairwise law checked by Monte Carlo. Stylised: one-dimensional Gaussian error, constant per-run bias, perfect reset.

projects.title: What does a simulator tuned on one-step odometry noise get wrong about drift, relocalisation and loop closure?
projects.summary: A traversal has a persistent bias plus white noise, so real error after T steps has variance σ12(ρT2+(1−ρ)T); a twin fitted to one-step increments, identical for every ρ, predicts σ12T and is off by exactly 1+(T−1)ρ. With 5% of step variance persistent, the twin’s relocalisation interval is 3.4× too long (real miss probability 51.6% against a claimed 5%), and a 3σ loop-closure gate tuned in it accepts true closures with probability 0.64 at T = 200 instead of 0.997; in a closed loop the rejections let error run away (RMS 8.8 m against 0.17 m calibrated). A calibrated gate accepts 97–99% of aliased closures once drift uncertainty exceeds the alias offset, and a variance ratio fitted at one loop length does not transfer to others. Stylised: 1-D Gaussian, assumed one-step-fitted twin, no real odometry data.

projects.title: How wrong is a safety margin certified in a Gaussian-disturbance simulator when real gusts are heavy-tailed?
projects.summary: A stabilised vehicle must stay in a corridor for T = 200 steps; the twin’s disturbances are Gaussian, the real ones Student-t with the same variance, so a variance fit cannot tell them apart. The twin’s certificate is exact (a union bound over its stationary tail), yet at the margin certified for δ = 0.01 the real failure probability is 0.29 (ν = 3) to 0.052 (ν = 8), and the margin the real system needs at δ = 0.001 is 7.3× to 1.25× the twin’s, a ratio that grows as δ shrinks. Inflating the twin variance to match real failure at δ = 0.05 still misses δ = 0.001 by 24×. A conformal margin from real episodes is valid but needs n ≥ 1/δ of them; a Hill tail fit to cheap one-step disturbances needs no failures and is below target in 93% of repeats at 2,000 samples. Stylised: 1-D linear system, i.i.d. disturbance, a simulated ‘real’ system, no flight data.

projects.title: How wrong is the thinnest obstacle a lidar twin certifies as detectable when real beam dropout is clustered?
projects.summary: A thin obstacle covers m adjacent lidar beams and is detected if at least k return. The twin drops beams independently at 10%; the real sensor drops them in bursts (a Markov chain with the same rate and lag-1 correlation λ). The exact miss law is a small DP, and for k = 1 the real/twin ratio is (1 + λ(1−p)/p)m−1. At the width certified for miss 10−3 (m = 3) the real miss is 0.041 (λ = 0.6) to 0.067 (λ = 0.8), and the claimed detection range is 4× to 8.3× too long. Inflating the drop rate to match one width is wrong at the others. Fitting the chain from a flat-target log recovers the median width but 40% of repeats still miss the target at 5,000 beams; two extra beams cut that to 1%. Stylised: one scan, a simulated ‘real’ sensor, no lidar data.

projects.title: Can a digital twin shorten a real-world safety certification?
projects.summary: Certifying a failure rate p < ε from n real trials with a twin-derived prior. The worst-case false-certification probability of any ‘certify iff k ≤ c’ rule is exactly P(Bin(n,ε) ≤ c), so by Karlin–Rubin the twin cannot cut real trials at a fixed level: at ε=0.01, δ=0.05 the exact test needs 299 zero-failure trials, a twin prior reaches 133 only at worst-case size 0.26, and the exact test held to the same size needs the same n (1057 vs 1057 for 90% power at p=ε/3). A weakly informative Jeffreys bound is already anti-conservative (size 0.147 at 191 trials). Optimistic twins inflate size, pessimistic ones (claim 2ε) block certification entirely, and the largest safe twin weight is about 90 twin-trial equivalents at n=299. Stylised: one Bernoulli failure rate, no continuous margins.

projects.title: How optimistic is the cost a planner quotes from its own twin rollouts?
projects.summary: A planner picks the cheapest of K plans by n twin rollouts each and explains the choice by quoting that simulated cost. With equal true costs the quote is low by exactly eK · s (eK = expected maximum of K standard normals: 0.56 at K=2, 1.16 at 5, 1.87 at 20; Monte-Carlo within 0.5%), a nominal 95% interval around it covers the true cost 88%, 78% and 60% of the time at K=5, 10, 20, and two identical plans are quoted a gap of 1.13 s. Reporting from fresh rollouts removes the bias exactly but costs selection quality (regret 0.069 to 0.104, best-plan rate 0.76 to 0.68 when 8 of 20 rollouts are diverted). It does not remove the twin’s own model error bk ~ N(0,τ2): the quoted-minus-real bias is −eKτ2/√(τ2+s2) (formula −0.531, simulated −0.530 at τ=0.5), so only real trials of the chosen plan give an honest real-cost quote. Stylised: independent Gaussian sample means (one skewed check: formula 7% high), no human study, no robot.

projects.title: How many retries does a grasp need when the simulator treats attempts as independent?
projects.summary: A pick skill is retried until success. The twin draws attempts independently at p = 0.6; in the “real” system each object has a latent success probability (Beta, same mean), so single-attempt validation cannot tell them apart while attempts on one object are correlated. Real failure after k attempts is exactly ∏(b+j)/(a+b+j), a power law k−a against the twin’s geometric law (matched to simulation). At the twin’s 6-attempt budget for δ = 0.01 (claimed 0.004) real failure is 0.010, 0.042 or 0.151 at correlation 0.05, 0.2 or 0.5, and the budget actually needed is 7, 13 or 571. The payoff cost of a wrong budget is mostly small (0–6%, 23% in one case) because the optimal give-up rule is closed-form. Two forced attempts per object identify the correlation, but a budget aimed at δ still needs a safety margin (met in 51–79% of repeats). Stylised.

projects.title: How optimistic is the best of K controllers chosen in a noisy digital twin?
projects.summary: Scoring K candidate controllers in a twin and deploying the argmin is a winner’s-curse selection. With score noise τ around true costs N(m, v2), the winner’s claimed cost is exactly m − √(v2+τ2) cK and its deployed cost m − v2cK/√(v2+τ2), so optimism τ2cK/√(v2+τ2) grows like √(2 ln K) (simulation agrees to within 0.03). With a fixed rollout budget the winner’s deployed cost is non-monotone in K (best K = 5, 8, 22 in three regimes; 5,000 candidates gain 5–10× less). In an exact-plant LQ twin (50 gains, 10 rollouts each) the claim is 8% below the deployed cost and below what any gain can achieve, though the Gaussian formula understates the size (optimism 0.0036 vs 0.0017 predicted). Fresh re-scoring fixes the claim but not the choice, empirical-Bayes shrinkage barely helps, and screen-then-verify cuts claim bias 4.5× (Gaussian model: regret 0.73 → 0.34 at K=100). Stylised: i.i.d. Gaussian score noise, one scalar plant, twin equal to the real plant.

projects.title: How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when evaluating a robot policy?
projects.summary: Using the twin as a control variate keeps the estimate unbiased whatever the twin's bias (twin-only error +0.700 vs +0.001) with exact variance σ<sub>R</sub>²((1−ρ²)/n + ρ²/N). Real and twin cannot share execution noise, so ρ is set by the observed scenario context: a faithful twin gets ρ=η but a noise-free twin gets ρ=√η (1.33× vs 2.0× real-sample equivalent at η=0.5). A twin is worth its compute only if c<sub>T</sub>/c<sub>R</sub> < (1−√(1−ρ²))²/ρ² (0.072 at ρ=0.5), and where twin bias favours the wrong policy, twin-only ranking is wrong while 86–125 real episodes per policy give a 90% correct order against 164 real-only. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, no robot data.

projects.title: How big a pilot decides whether a biased digital twin is worth using?
projects.summary: The twin pays iff its correlation with the real return exceeds ρ*=2√r/(1+r) (0.426 at cost ratio r=0.05), and the gain is linear in ρ−ρ* there, so a small pilot's wrong calls are frequent but cheap (probability 0.36–0.11 at ρ=0.5 for m=10–160 pairs, regret 0.004–0.016 of real-only variance). Decision regret follows f·slope·(1−ρ*<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>/(2m) (simulated/law 0.63 at m=10, 1.00 at 160) and plug-in allocation costs ≈0.27–0.30/m extra variance. The adaptive two-stage design (pilot reused) stays unbiased (|bias| ≤ 0.002 against twin bias 0.7) with 95% intervals covering 0.946–0.955. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, asymptotic law, no robot data.

projects.title: Does giving two policies the same seed in a digital twin actually pair them?
projects.summary: Common random numbers pair two policies only while their read pointers into the random stream stay aligned. If one policy consumes an extra draw with probability q per step, the paired correlation is exactly ρ = ∑t∑d Bin(t,q)(d) wtwt+d/∑wt² (matched to simulation within 0.012). A flat 20-step score keeps ρ=0.95/0.77 at q=0.05/0.3, but a terminal-only score has ρ=(1−q)T (0.36/0.001). Sizing a comparison as if seeds stayed synchronised (n=12) gives power 0.85 to 0.11 against a nominal 0.90; keying each draw by (episode, step) restores ρ=1. Stylised: Gaussian per-step noise, policies differing only in draw consumption, no robot data.

projects.title: What overshoot does a controller tuned in a fixed-step digital twin really have?
projects.summary: A twin's integrator adds or removes damping the plant does not have. Per-step pole moduli are exact (real e<sup>−hc</sup>; explicit 1−hc+h²k; semi-implicit 1−hc; implicit 1/(1+hc+h²k)), and the first-order damping bias of explicit and implicit Euler changes sign at ζ=1/√2 (measured 0.742→0.711 and 0.675→0.703 as h falls 0.2→0.025). Tuned to 10% overshoot in the twin, the real plant overshoots 0.105–0.192 (semi-implicit and implicit, h=0.05–0.4) while forward Euler is conservative (0.091–0.036); at a 1% target the semi-implicit twin under-claims by up to 4.9×. The excess halves with h (first order); Richardson extrapolation of the twin’s overshoot at fixed gain recovers the real value to 0.0003–0.0012, and re-tuning with substeps costs ×4 to ×32. Stylised: one linear oscillator, textbook integrators (not any engine’s scheme), overshoot read from samples, no robot data.

projects.title: What does a too-narrow scenario generator do to a digital twin's estimate of a rare failure?
projects.summary: With real scenarios x~N(0,1), failure iff x>a, and a twin generator of width s, the raw twin claims Q(a/s) and the reweighted (importance-sampling) estimate has per-sample second moment sτQ(a/τ), τ2=s2/(2s2−1), finite only for s2>½. In a braking example (P=1.2×10−3) a generator 0.6× too narrow claims 2.1×10−7 and reported zero failures in all 4,000 simulated runs of 2,000 scenarios; a wide one over-claims but reweighting repairs it, with optimal width ≈1.05a needing 2,179 runs for 10% error against 83,459 for plain Monte Carlo. A defensive mixture with the real prior makes a narrow twin's variance finite but no better than plain Monte Carlo. Stylised: one-dimensional Gaussian scenarios, known threshold and density, correct twin failure indicator.

projects.title: What does a state estimator tuned in a twin with the wrong noise levels cost in the real world?
projects.summary: For a scalar Kalman filter (plant x′=ax+w, sensor y=x+v) the real error under the twin’s gain K is exactly ((1−K)2Q+K2R)/(1−(1−K)2a2). With a=0.9 and Q=R=1, a twin 10× too quiet claims MSE 0.215 but the real MSE is 1.32 (+121%), while one 10× too noisy is slightly pessimistic (+42%); at 100× the quiet twin costs 5.0 against 0.64, and for a random walk quiet-twin regret grows as m−1/2. Regret is locally c(ln m)2. Negative result: for an unstable plant the twin’s gain never destabilises the filter. The lag-1 innovation covariance is zero iff the gain is optimal, and a one-shot moment retune from real innovations cut regret from 2.15 to 0.026 at n=200 and 0.0002 at n=25,000 (simulation, ∼1/n). Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian system, stationary, known dynamics.

projects.title: What does a controller designed in a twin with the wrong actuator gain cost in the real world?
projects.summary: For a scalar LQR controller (plant x′=ax+bu+w) the real cost under the twin’s gain K is exactly (q+rK2)W/(1−(a−bK)2). With a=0.9, a twin that believes the actuator is half as strong claims 1.245 but costs 1.508 (+40%); at 0.2× the real loop is unstable while the twin claims a finite cost. Unlike an estimator, a controller has an instability cliff (m < a/(a+1) as r→0), which is a band when control is penalised, and a too-strong twin is the safer error (+20% vs +40% at a factor of 2). Negative result: running the twin’s controller on the real system identifies only the closed-loop pole, not a and b; with dither the least-squares covariance is closed-form and the retune regret matches a delta-method law (∝1/n), while dither costs performance and its optimum shrinks with the data budget. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, stationary, known a.

projects.title: How long does a simulator without actuator limits say an unstable plant stays in control?
projects.summary: An unstable scalar plant (a=1.2) with a saturating actuator loses control when |x| exceeds U/(a−1). A twin with an unlimited actuator, running its own LQR gain, overstates the mean time to loss of control by 6,295× at noise sd 1 (1.5×106 vs 245 steps), 106× at 0.8, and still 5.7× at 2. ln T is linear in 1/s2 with slope ≈3.7 on the real plant against ≈12.7–13.2 for the twin (large-deviation value 12.4), so the gap is exponential, not a constant factor. Both are maximised at the deadbeat gain, but the twin’s time-to-failure varies five orders of magnitude across gains against 2× on the real plant. Exit times solve an integral equation (grid- and Monte-Carlo-checked; twin values above 1010 unresolved). Stylised: scalar plant, one parameter set; the real exponent is empirical.

projects.title: What does a Kalman filter tuned in an ideal-sensor twin cost on a quantizing real sensor?
projects.summary: A twin whose sensor is ideal (y=x+v) tunes the gain for variance R, but the real sensor rounds to a step D. In simulation (a=0.9, Q=1) the twin’s gain costs +11% at D=4 for R=1, and up to +64% when R=0.01. Retuning on R+D2/12 (Sheppard) lands within 1% of the best gain in all 12 configurations, but its closed-form MSE claim under-predicts the real error by 28–43% once D exceeds the state’s scale (1.61 vs 2.82 at D=8, R=0.01). Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian plant, fixed gain, one seed per cell.

projects.title: How should a simulation budget be split across twin fidelities?
projects.summary: A twin runs at several fixed-step fidelities (n=2l+1 Euler steps). Multilevel Monte Carlo telescopes the finest-level answer over coupled pairs sharing scenario draws, with allocation Nl ∝ √(Vl/Cl). For a smooth terminal state (bias rate α=1.000, variance rate β=2.001, cost rate 1) it needs 3.6× fewer steps than one fine twin at RMSE 10−2 and 897× fewer at 3×10−5. For a failure probability the variance only halves per level (β=1.000), so multilevel loses at loose targets (0.4× at 3×10−2), breaks even near 10−3 and reaches 7.7× at 10−4. Equal samples per level cost 156× (smooth) and 3.9× (failure) the optimum; a coarse twin alone is off by 10–48% however many runs. Stylised: one scalar linear system, exact level moments.

projects.title: How many real steps does a twin-pretrained policy save, and which twin errors does fine-tuning inherit?
projects.summary: On a quadratic real loss with SGD noise, the expected loss after k real steps from a twin start is exact (matched to Monte Carlo within 0.3%). A twin start with 0.6× the cold-start error saves 64–67% of the steps to every target from 8× to 1.2× the SGD floor; at equal error it saves nothing and at 1.5× it costs 138 extra steps (negative transfer). For any curvature spectrum the loss left by a twin error of norm b is at most b2/(4eηk), attained by the direction λ*=1/(2ηk), so twin error decays as 1/k, not geometrically. At the same initial loss, an error in the stiffest direction needs 13 steps to reach 2× the floor and one in the flattest 1,541. Stylised: fixed offset, isotropic noise, no robot data.

projects.title: How far ahead should a controller planned in a twin with the wrong plant pole look?
projects.summary: A receding-horizon controller uses the H-step gain of a twin whose pole is m× the real one; the real cost of that fixed gain is exact (matched to simulation within 0.3%). When the twin overstates the pole the gain rises with H past the real optimum, so cost is not monotone in the horizon: at m=2 (a=0.9, r=1) the real cost is 1.81 at H=2 and 3.97 at H=60 against an optimum of 1.48, and the saving rises from 12% to 91% as control cost goes from 0.1 to 20. The twin cannot see this (its own claim falls from 9.5 to 3.5 as H grows, ranking horizons backwards); the two-step controller stays stable up to m=(1+a)(r+b2q)/(abq) (4.22 vs 2.51 for H=60 at r=1). A terminal cost equal to the twin’s Riccati solution removes the effect. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, only the pole wrong, best horizon chosen with the real cost known.

projects.title: How should cheap biased twin samples be weighted against scarce real ones?
projects.summary: For a mean estimated from n real and m twin samples with twin bias δ, the optimal weight and MSE are exact and the twin is worth at most σ2/δ2 real samples however large m is (e.g. 157.5 of a 160 cap at m=104). Equal-weight pooling beats real-only iff δ2 < σ2/n + σ2/m, so more twin data narrows the safe range (3.99× worse than real-only at δ=2√a). Estimating the bias from the data is costly: the plug-in weight is worse than real-only for large bias (peak 1.24×), and a 5% pretest peaks at 2.41×. Stylised: scalar Gaussian, constant bias, no robot data.

projects.title: How much load can a shared lab instrument carry when its twin assumes exponential service?
projects.summary: With Poisson arrivals and one server, the mean wait is exactly ρ(1+c2)/(2(1−ρ)) service times (Pollaczek–Khinchine; matched to a 1.5-million-job simulation within one standard error), so a twin with exponential service is off by (1+c2)/2 at every load. At a mean-wait SLA of 2 service times the twin admits ρ=0.667 while the real instrument admits 0.444 (c2=4) or 0.133 (c2=25): real mean waits 2.5× to 13× the SLA, and 11.7× the twin’s tail-exceedance claim at c2=4. With a Pareto tail of index below 2 the real mean wait is infinite. A negative repair result: a plug-in c2 fitted from n logged service times violates the SLA in 70–89% of repeats for n=25–1600, and a 90% bootstrap bound still 46% at n=1600. Stylised (Poisson arrivals, one server, simulated “real” instrument).

projects.title: How much smoothing does a differentiable twin of a hard contact event need, and what does it cost?
projects.summary: A hard success edge has zero real gradient, so a smoothed twin is the only learning signal. The twin optimum overshoots the edge, θ ≈ τln(R/(2cmτ)) (within 5% at τ=0.02), and gradient ascent from the nominal pose is trapped below τc=0.105 (real regret 0.75) while above τu=R/(8cm)=0.25 the twin optimum falls below the real edge and regret jumps to 0.98. Annealing τ from 0.2 crosses the trap (regret 0.08 at τ=0.02; the real plant alone needs 161 to 3.5×106 evaluations). With an uncertain real edge the overshoot is a safety margin: the best trainable width is within 0.0014 expected regret of the Bayes-best pose, but reachable margins are capped at 0.168 and annealing to zero width discards the margin. Stylised (one parameter, logistic smoother, deterministic ascent, simulated “real” plant).

projects.title: How many redundant sensors does a twin with independent errors say a robot needs?
projects.summary: Redundant sensors that share an error source have pairwise correlation ρ; the equal-weight fused variance is exactly σ2(1+(n−1)ρ)/n, so a twin with independent errors understates the fused std by √(1+(n−1)ρ), n sensors are worth fewer than 1/ρ independent ones, and no fleet beats σ√ρ. For a target std of 0.25σ the twin says 16 sensors; the real fleet needs 30 at ρ=0.03, 77 at 0.05, 376 at 0.06 and none at 0.0625 or above. A 3-σ gate sized from the twin false-alarms 8.6× too often at ρ=0.05 (n=16). Repair from calibration logs is mixed: the estimated ρ is unbiased, but a plug-in fleet size misses the target in about half of repeats; a 90% bootstrap upper bound misses in 8.5% (T=400) at almost twice the sensors, and short logs cannot support the target. Stylised: equal-variance Gaussian errors with one common factor, simulated fleet, no sensor data.

projects.title: How much is one long digital-twin run worth when its output is serially correlated?
projects.summary: Twin output such as queue waits is autocorrelated, but a run is usually summarised as mean ± 1.96 s/√n. For AR(1) output the run-mean variance is exact (matched to simulation), so 1000 draws at φ=0.9 are worth 53. For an M/M/1 lab instrument the variance of the run mean is 9.7×, 33× and 363× the iid value at ρ=0.5, 0.7, 0.9: from 104 jobs the naive 95% interval covers the true mean wait 53%, 26% and 9% of the time, and a twin “certifies” an SLA of 8 against a true mean of 9 in 26% of runs. Higher load needs a longer run (470 jobs by the iid formula, 170,268 exactly at ρ=0.9). Batch means restore coverage (94–95%) only when batches outlast the correlation time; it is 53.5% at φ=0.99 and 82.5% at ρ=0.9, n=104. Stylised (Gaussian AR(1) and M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

projects.title: How much of a digital-twin run should be thrown away because it started in the wrong state?
projects.summary: A twin started from an empty queue or a nominal sensor value is biased at first. For AR(1) output the bias and variance of the run mean are exact (0.300 vs 0.300 simulated at φ=0.9, n=100), and the MSE-optimal warm-up is about one relaxation time 1/(1−φ) with a gain of at most 1.5× and 1.03× once n is about a hundred relaxation times. An M/M/1 instrument started empty underestimates the mean wait by 21%, 6% and 1.2% at ρ=0.9 with 500, 2000 and 104 jobs, but at 5000 jobs the bias (−0.14) is far below the run-to-run RMSE (2.4). Negative result: fixed deletion does not lower RMSE, and MSER-5 truncation leaves a larger bias (−0.77), covers 61% against 72% for no truncation, and passes a violating system 28% of the time against 18%. Stylised (Gaussian AR(1), M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

projects.title: How wrong is a twin's localisation error when real ranges have non-line-of-sight bias?
projects.summary: A twin draws anchor ranges as true distance plus Gaussian noise; real sites also have long-biased NLOS ranges. On a ring of anchors the rms position error is exactly GDOP·√(σ2+p(2−p)m2) (1.105 vs law 1.095 m at p=0.1, n=6), 4.5× and 7.3× the twin's at p=0.1 and 0.3, with zero mean. A blocked side is a bias the linear formula predicts to about 0.02 m per coordinate (0.924 vs 0.930 m) while the twin predicts none. Sized on the twin, a 1 m / 95% corridor needs 4 anchors; the NLOS site needs about 28 (p=0.1) or 46 (p=0.2), and the 4-anchor ring leaves the corridor 34.7% of the time instead of 5%. Dropping the largest-residual anchor cuts rms error 0.947→0.414 m at p=0.1 but costs 24% with no NLOS. Stylised: 2-D ring, iid exponential NLOS, simulated site, no sensor data.

projects.title: Can a twin identified from logs of the deployed controller tell you whether a different controller is stable?
projects.summary: A twin fitted to closed-loop logs predicts the pole under a new gain k′ with sd (σ/√n)√((k−k′)2/τ2+1/v), set by the dither τ: held-out one-step error is 1.00–1.005σ2 at every τ, while the predicted pole's sd goes 0.037 to 0.82 (matching the formula to a few percent). With no dither the minimum-norm fit gets b̂=−0.22 (true +1) and certifies a real-unstable gain in 100% of fits. Point-rule false certification is 3–48%; the OLS upper bound cuts it to 0.1–4.7% but rarely certifies a good gain at low dither (5–9%). A predicted-pole sd of 0.05 needs τ=1.23 / 0.40 / 0.16 at n=200 / 1000 / 5000. Stylised: scalar linear plant, simulated data.

projects.title: How much of a digital twin's error is that it was fitted to finite real data, however long it is simulated?
projects.summary: A twin fitted to n real interarrival and service times has a steady-state wait that is one fixed number, so its error is input error that more simulation cannot remove. The relative sd is √(1+(2−ρ)2)/((1−ρ)√n) (0.255 vs 0.257 simulated), so a 10% sd needs 1300 / 22 100 observations per stream at ρ=0.5 / 0.9. The fitted twin is unstable with exact probability P[F(2n,2n) ≥ 1/ρ] (0.370 at ρ=0.9, n=20). Used as truth, the point twin certifies a 10%-violated SLA in 36–46% of fits; the delta-method bound under-covers at high load (0.87–0.89), while bootstrap and posterior bounds reach 0.94 and cut false certification to 2–5% at a large power cost. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data.

projects.title: For a fixed budget, how much should a fitted digital twin spend on real data and how much on simulation length?
projects.summary: A twin fitted to n real observations and simulated for m jobs has relative variance a(ρ)/n + b(ρ)/m about the real wait (Whitt’s M/M/1 constant matched to simulation: 30.4 vs 29.0). One real interarrival–service pair carries the information of about two simulated jobs at any load (ratio 2.23 → 2.00), so the optimal real-data share of a budget is interior: 0.97 / 0.81 / 0.57 as a simulated job costs 0.001 / 0.05 / 0.5 of a real observation. In a full pipeline the optimal split has 2.5× lower RMSE than 20% real data. A simulation-only confidence interval is for the twin, not the system: its coverage of the real wait falls from 0.79 to 0.17 as the run grows from 200 to 50 000 jobs, while adding the input variance gives 0.92–0.95 for runs of 1000 or more. Stylised: M/M/1, simulated data, first-order variances.

projects.title: When should a twin run that counts rare failures stop?
projects.summary: Running a safety twin “until the interval is narrow” stops on zero failures, because p̂=0 has Wald half-width 0: with a target of p/5, 90% of runs stop at the first check for p=10−3 (99% at 10−4), the interval covers p in 9.6% of runs and the reported rate is 10× too low. Running until m failures (inverse sampling) makes (m−1)/(N−1) exactly unbiased while m/N is about m/(m−1) too high, gives relative sd ≈1/√(m−2) whatever p is (m=102 for 10%; measured 0.101), and an exact interval covers 95.0–95.5%. A fixed run planned for p=10−3 delivers a 20% relative half-width there but 63% at 10−4. A one-failure minimum alone restores Wald coverage in this configuration, because the target already forces ~96 failures. Stylised (iid Bernoulli failures, faithful twin, no run cap).

projects.title: What stopping distance can a twin with independent terrain cells certify?
projects.summary: Braking on Gamma-distributed patch friction has an exact incomplete-gamma law. A twin drawing 100 independent cells across the stopping distance certifies 1.17× the mean-friction distance at level 10<sup>−3</sup>; on real terrain with 1, 3 or 10 patches across it the exceedance is 0.44, 0.33 and 0.18, and finer twin cells make it worse. The mean stopping distance is nearly right (1.00–1.32×) while the tail is not. Matching the measured patch count restores the level; overstating it 2× gives 16× the claimed risk. Stylised.

projects.title: What approach speed can a lidar twin that returns every beam certify?
projects.summary: Scanning-lidar detection of a thin obstacle has an exact random-phase beam-count law and a product-over-scans miss probability (matched to a beam-pattern Monte Carlo). A twin calibrated on the mean return rate but with independent beams has no whole-scan fades; the real miss probability cannot fall below sn for n scans. At level 10−3 the twin certifies 13.3 and 12.9 m/s against the real 12.0 and 10.9 (fade rates 0.3, 0.5), with real miss probability 0.09–0.125, about 100× the level; the gap vanishes for early-visible obstacles and reverses sign when several returns are required. The probabilities are off by orders of magnitude but the speed by only 10–30%, because miss probability is a cliff in speed. A few hundred calibration scans repair it. Stylised.

projects.title: How do you estimate a one-in-a-million failure from a twin you can only run a thousand times?
projects.summary: Shifting the twin's disturbances and reweighting failures is unbiased for any shift, with an exact variance enθ²Q((b+nθ)/√n) (5.53 vs 5.51 simulated). At the optimal shift, 10% error at p=10−6 takes 535 runs instead of 108. But the shift is a narrow target: half the optimum costs 23× the variance, twice the optimum 1.7×105×, and a shift tuned for one design is 1.6–17.6× worse at thresholds 0.8–1.5× away. The usual 95% interval covers 94.9% at the optimum but 2.8% at twice it, and only the effective sample size warns. Stylised: Gaussian additive disturbances, constant shift, no field data.

projects.title: Which ego-velocity estimator should a radar twin choose when the real scene has moving targets?
projects.summary: Radar ego-velocity from n Doppler returns. In a static-world twin least squares beats the median by exactly π/2, so the twin picks the mean; in a scene where a fraction ε of returns come from moving targets (extra offset sd τσ) the mean’s variance is exactly 1 + ετ2 times the twin’s claim and the median’s exact variance is a one-dimensional integral, both matched to simulation. The twin’s choice is wrong on a band of ε (τ=10: 0.006–0.97; τ=3: 0.086–0.83; τ=1: never); at ε=0.1, τ=10 the mean has 5.8× the median’s variance and the twin’s 95% interval covers 48.7% of the time. 2-D least squares scales the same way. A residual-kurtosis test needs about 50 returns to detect it at ε=0.1, τ=10, and hundreds at ε=0.02, τ=3. Stylised: zero-mean Gaussian contamination, no RANSAC, no radar data.

projects.title: A radar twin with no Doppler folding certifies an ego-velocity estimator at every speed: what does the folding sensor do to it, and when can it be unfolded?
projects.summary: Real radar radial speeds wrap modulo 2vu (vu=10 m/s); the twin’s do not. The twin-tuned least-squares ego-speed estimator has RMSE 0.022 m/s in the twin and on the real sensor up to 9.5 m/s, then 0.18 (9.8), 1.9 (10) and 14.9 m/s (12). Its large-n bias is exact in closed form (−14.94 at 12 m/s, simulated −14.92) and saturates at −D, D=2vuΣc/Σc2, once every target is one fold off. A wrapped-cost grid search restores the twin’s accuracy to 60 m/s with no mode errors, provided the azimuths are diverse: the nearest wrong speed has residual energy 4vu2(n−(Σc)2/Σc2), independent of speed, and Φ(−√E/2σ) matches Monte Carlo (0.061 vs 0.054 at ±8°); at ±5° the search picks the wrong fold in 120 of 300 scenes. Stylised: stationary scene, known azimuths and vu, Gaussian noise, no multi-PRF.

projects.title: How many real trials before “the twin passed validation” means anything for a rare failure?
projects.summary: A twin states a failure probability q; the real rate is c q. An exact two-sided binomial difference test “passes” a twin that is 3× wrong with probability 0.81 at 500 trials (q = 10−3), and rejecting a 2× error with 80% power needs about 11 real failures, independent of q (normal approximation 9.9). Passing barely moves the odds that a twin is off by 2× (0.325 prior, 0.31 after passing at 0.3 expected failures). An equivalence test (TOST) caps false validation at 5% but needs about 20, 58 and 178 real failures for margins 2, 1.5 and 1.25, so certifying a rare-failure twin within 2× takes about 20/q real trials. Stylised: one Bernoulli failure, known q, no scenario shift, illustrative prior.

projects.title: How safe is a robot's goal inference when its commit threshold was tuned against a simulated human?
projects.summary: A robot commits to one of two goals when the evidence lead reaches h (a sequential test on binary motion cues); against a human of cue accuracy p the wrong-goal probability is exactly 1/(1+rh), r=p/(1−p), matched to simulation. A threshold set for error 10−3 in a twin with ps=0.9 gives real error 3.9× / 33× / 165× the target at p=0.8 / 0.7 / 0.6, while a too-irrational twin (ps=0.6) is safe but 2.0–4.5× slower. A heterogeneous population (sd 0.08–0.10) doubles the error of the mean-human threshold, and humans with p<½ put a floor under any threshold. Calibrating ps from n real cues misses the target with probability 0.38 / 0.42 / 0.33 / 0.30 / 0.14 at n=10 / 20 / 50 / 200 / 1000; a lower-confidence-bound design cuts that to ≤4% at the cost of time. Stylised: two goals, i.i.d. binary cues, simulated humans.

projects.title: How much does a twin's perfectly synchronised sensor clock over-promise a fused estimate?
projects.summary: Two sensors observe a smooth signal (length scale ℓ); the second has a clock offset δ and jitter s, which the twin does not simulate. The added variance is exactly g = 2σ2[1−(1+s2/ℓ2)−1/2e−δ2/2(ℓ2+s2)] ≈ σ2(δ2+s2)/ℓ2 (matched to simulation within 0.5%), so inverse-variance fusion designed in the twin has real MSE 1 + ag/(b(a+b)) times its claim: +44% at a 0.3ℓ offset, +118% at 0.5ℓ, and worse than the reference sensor alone beyond 0.225ℓ. The more accurate the delayed sensor, the more it hurts. Randomising the twin’s clock at the right variance recovers the optimal weight; no randomisation costs up to 29%, a range 4× too wide only 1–4%. Stylised: very smooth signal, static weights, offset known, no real logs.

projects.title: What does a twin get wrong when its gain is fitted from a noisy logged input, and does more data fix it?
projects.summary: Regressing the plant output on a logged input that carries sensor noise attenuates the fitted gain by the reliability ratio λ = σu2/(σu2+σv2) exactly (0.800 vs 0.802 simulated at λ=0.8). It is bias, not variance, so more data makes it worse: the twin's own 95% interval covers the true gain 53% / 15% / 0% at n=20 / 50 / 200 while covering the attenuated value 94–97%, and the twin's fit residuals are exactly uncorrelated with its regressor, so nothing warns. A feedforward controller built on it overshoots the real plant by exactly 1/λ (1.25× at λ=0.8, 2× at 0.5). A known-noise correction or a second independent measurement as instrument removes the bias (RMSE 0.20 to 0.02–0.05 at n=200–1000), but a 20% misjudged noise variance leaves a ±5% bias and at n=20 with λ=0.5 the repairs are far worse than the biased fit. Stylised: scalar Gaussian plant, simulated “real” system.

projects.title: What does a twin with no actuator deadband promise a proportional loop, and what does the real one do?
projects.summary: With a deadband d the real servo loop rests at exactly |x| = d/k (0.500 at d=0.2, k=0.4) while the twin converges to zero, so the twin certifies tolerances the real loop never meets and needs k ≥ d/ε, which fails beyond k = 1. A linear twin fitted from Gaussian excitation of std s recovers 2Q(d/s) (Stein’s lemma; 0.0457 vs 0.0455 at s=0.5), an excitation-dependent gain, while the small-signal gain is 0. Bisection needs about 8 real probes to cut the stall 0.784 → 0.0005, with exact residuals (d−d̂)/k under-compensated and a period-2 chatter (d̂−d)/(2−k) over-compensated. Stylised: scalar integrator, noiseless, k ≤ 1.

projects.title: Does measurement noise, or dither, hide an actuator deadband the twin lacks?
projects.summary: At K=0.5, d=0.1 the linear twin’s exact stationary rms is s√(K/(2−K)); the real deadband loop is 27× worse at s=0.01 (0.1591 vs 0.0058) but 0.37× at s=0.05 (0.0107 vs 0.0289), because noise dithers the actuator, so a validation in the high-noise regime would call the deadband harmless. Deliberate dither removes the noise-free stall (rms 0.2000 to 0.0001 at a=d) but only hurts at s=0.05 (0.0103 to 0.0226), and under noise mild under-compensation of the width beats the exact width (0.0053 vs 0.0116 at s=0.02). Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar integrator, single-seed simulations without confidence intervals.

projects.title: How large a manoeuvre can a twin without an actuator rate limit be trusted for?
projects.summary: The real loop x⁺ = x + a⁺, with the command rate-limited to r per step, is scale-invariant: it depends only on ρ = x0/r, while the first-order twin does not. The twin is exact iff x0 ≤ r/k (difference 0 at 0.999×, 0.1–0.6% of x0 at 1.01×). Beyond that the real loop overshoots the target (0.23 of x0 at ρ=100, 0.90 at 104, k=0.3) and settles in O(ρ) steps (29418 at ρ=105 vs the twin’s 13). For k=1/n the overshoot threshold is empirically ρ*=2n(2n−1) (not proved); avoiding overshoot needs a rate limit 12–38× lower than keeping the twin exact. Stylised: scalar plant, no noise or delay.

projects.title: Does a twin with a rigid drivetrain miss the hunting cycle caused by gear backlash?
projects.summary: On a discrete PI loop the rigid twin has spectral radius 0.71–0.89 and converges, yet the real loop with a gap of half-width h settles on a limit cycle of motor amplitude 1.30–2.94h that scales exactly with h (1.302317 for h=0.01, 1, 100). The backlash describing function is an excitation-dependent gain (0.21 at A/h=1.2, 0.99 at 30) with a phase lag, and harmonic balance predicts the cycle but overestimates its amplitude by 6.7–10.1%. Negative result: the loop is bistable in some settings (hunting 1.165h from small starts, converging from large steps), so a large-step validation can pass a configuration that hunts. Follow-up to the deadband twin. Stylised: scalar loop, symmetric known gap, noiseless.

projects.title: How wrong is the stopping distance of a twin that models friction as purely viscous?
projects.summary: With Coulomb friction c the real coast-down stops in finite time with exact distance (m/b)[v0−(c/b)ln(1+b v0/c)] (RK4 agreement 9×10−9), while the viscous twin only decays exponentially (6.5 s to reach 10−3 vs 1.95 s real). The least-squares gain b+cE[v]/E[v2] depends on the logged speed range (1.23 on [1,3], 3.44 on [0.05,0.3]); fitted on [1,3] the twin overestimates stopping distance ×1.8 at v0=1 and ×17 at 0.05, is exact at 7.34 and underestimates above. Negative result: no single viscous gain does better than 0.87 worst relative error over [0.05,3], while an affine fit recovers (b,c) exactly. Stylised: one mass, noiseless logs.

projects.title: Does a twin with correct sliding friction still miss stick-slip hunting from static friction?
projects.summary: Unit mass under PID, frictionless twin stable (error below 1e-58). With Fs=Fc (sliding friction identified correctly) the real loop converges in all 15 cases tried, so that twin validates. With a stiction excess ΔF=Fs−Fc it hunts in stick-slip at 0.54–0.93 ΔF/kp in four of five gain settings, independent of Fc (0 to 20) and of the start, falling with damping; one setting (kd=4, ki=5) converges. Scaling is bit-exact for power-of-two scales but the cycle is unique only to about three digits. Negative result: a 1000 s run can show a motionless “converged” error for large Fc/ki while a 20 000 s run still hunts; the amplitude constant has no closed form here. Follow-up to the backlash twin. Stylised: unit mass, Coulomb plus static friction, noiseless.

projects.title: How much bandwidth can a controller tuned in a twin with an instantaneous actuator really have?
projects.summary: Unit mass under PD control with a first-order actuator lag τ the twin omits. The twin’s loop is stable for every gain; the real loop is stable iff τ<τ*=kd/kp=2ζ/ωn (Routh, agreeing with the roots in 168 of 168 cases), hunts at exactly the twin’s own ωn, and grows at ωn2/(2(1+4ζ2)) per unit excess lag (formula, numeric slope and simulation agree). “Faster is better” fails: at τ=0.05, ζ=0.7 the real decay rate peaks at 4.8 (ωn≈8) and is zero at ωn=28 where the twin promises 19.6; the poles sum to −1/τ, so no gains decay faster than 1/(3τ). Mild lag is nearly invisible in a step test (twin RMS error ≈0.04 ε). Companion to the slew, deadband and backlash twins. Stylised: linear, one lag, noiseless.

projects.title: How high a bandwidth does a rigid-body twin let you push when the real joint is flexible?
projects.summary: A twin with one rigid inertia says the PD loop is stable at every bandwidth. With load-side sensing the real two-mass loop is unstable above εc = w/ws, the smallest root of a cubic in modal damping δ and twin damping ratio ζ: exactly independent of the mass ratio, ≈ δ/ζ for small δ (0.0143, 0.0714, 0.286 for δ = 0.01, 0.05, 0.2 at ζ = 0.7), and unstable at every gain with no modal damping. Motor-side (collocated) sensing was stable at all 7 320 grid points, so the twin is right about one sensor placement and wrong about the other. Twin and real step responses differ by under 1% at 0.9 εc, so ordinary validation gives no warning; a twin that overstates δ by a factor f certifies εc high by the same factor, and a design at fraction m of the certified bandwidth tolerates f ≈ 1/m. Stylised: one flexible mode, linear, PD only, continuous-time, noiseless.

projects.title: Does a twin that models each axis alone certify gains that actuator coupling destabilises?
projects.summary: For a two-axis loop x’ = x − kGx with cross-gain c, the stable-gain limit is 2/(1+√p) (p=c12c21≥0) or 2/(1+|p|) (p<0) instead of the twin’s 2, so a twin-certified 10% margin (k=1.8) fails at c=1/9, and no positive gain is stable once √p≥1. The twin-deadbeat gain has real rate √|p|, not 0 (6–270 steps to 10−6 for c=0.1–0.95 vs 1). A diagonal gain fitted from logs is 1+cρ for input correlation ρ (Monte Carlo matches to four digits), giving real rate c(1+ρ)/(1+cρ) (0.300 at ρ=0, 0.461 at ρ=1); the unbiased full fit has variance ∝ 1/(1−ρ2) (verified within 5%), so near-collinear logs make coupling unidentifiable while the per-axis fit returns a confident wrong gain. Follow-up to the control twin. Stylised: linear constant coupling, two axes, noiseless plant.

projects.title: A twin with an unlimited actuator says a PI step response ignores step size: what does the real loop with a command limit do?
projects.summary: Integrator plant under PI control, real actuator limited to |u|≤U with constant load d; the twin has neither. The twin is exact iff kpx0≤U (zero deviation up to x0=0.714), so gentle step tests certify it. Beyond that the integrator winds up to exactly x02/(2U): overshoot rises from the twin’s 21% to 74%, 93%, 97% and the settling time from 4.9 to 17, 165, 944 (x0/U=5, 20, 50); a load d≥U is never rejected and settling blows up as d→U. “Faster is better” fails: the twin’s settling time falls 32× over ωn=0.25–8 while the real one is best near ωn=1 and rises to 77; conditional integration recovers most of it. Companion to the lag and slew twins. Stylised: one integrator, static limit, noiseless.

projects.title: A fixed-step twin of a bouncing ball: how wrong are its restitution and time to rest, and does calibrating on the first bounce fix it?
projects.summary: Truth is closed form: infinitely many impacts in the finite Zeno time T=(v1/g)(1+e)/(1−e), with d ln T/de=2/(1−e2) (10.5 at e=0.9, 100 at 0.99). A semi-implicit-Euler twin with a penetration test has an apparent restitution biased by the step with scheme-dependent sign (true 0.9: 0.886, 0.895, 0.879 at dt=10−2) and its time to come to rest is off by −19.6%, +4.0%, −30.8% (e=0.9; up to 47% at e=0.95), first-order in dt and 0.1–0.3% at 10−4. The restitution bias explains most of the clamp error (predicted −14.9%, measured −19.6%), but fitting e on the first rebound is not a reliable repair: it helps the clamp twin at dt=10−2 (−19.6% to −4.8%), does nothing at finer steps and makes the mirror twin worse (+4.0% to +53%). Twin impact counts (238–688) are mostly floor chatter against 43–87 resolvable bounces. Stylised: one dimension, constant restitution, rigid contact, closed-form real system; the crude interpolated-contact variant is the worst here.

projects.title: Does a twin fitted to the sensor-delay histogram certify gains that bursty delay makes unstable?
projects.summary: Scalar loop x[n+1]=x[n]−k x[n−dn]+w[n] with random delay; the twin has the same marginal delay law (constant mean: stable iff k<2 sin(π/(2(2d+1)))). Independent jitter moves the mean-square limit little and in either direction (1.000 for {0,2}, 0.952 for {0,1,2}, 0.668 vs the twin’s 0.618 for {0,1,2,3,4}); for {0,2} with P(d=2)=p it fits k(k+1)=1/p. Persistence, invisible in the histogram, is the large effect: at fixed marginal the limit falls 1.000→0.875→0.672→0.624 at lag-1 autocorrelation ρ=0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 (towards the worst-case constant delay’s 0.618); a twin-certified k=0.9 is unstable from ρ=0.435, and below the limit the variance at k=0.6 inflates from 2.56 to 6.26 (ρ=0.9) and 15.2 (ρ=0.99). Almost-sure stability (simulated limit ≈1.84) is insensitive to ρ, so which stability the safety claim needs decides whether persistence matters. Companion to the latency twin. Stylised: scalar plant, sticky-redraw delay, Monte-Carlo almost-sure limits (one seed).

projects.title: Does a twin with no gravity certify PD gains that sag, or cannot hold a pose at all?
projects.summary: A pendulum under PD control u=kp(θ*−θ)−kdω; the twin omits gravity and promises zero error at every gain. The real hold sags to the root of kp(θ*−θ)=g sinθ nearest the target (RK4 agrees to six digits; 0.182 rad at kp=4, θ*=1), falling only as ≈1/kp. Holding upright is stable iff kp>g: below it the arm settles 0.2–1.9 rad away, and just above it the basin is tiny (0.116 rad at 1.02g, 0.519 at 1.05g, none below 3 rad from 1.1g; numerical scan). A gravity feedforward with calibration error leaves a sag linear in (g(g−gff)minus;gff) (±0.0185 rad at ±10%). Companion to the lag and flex twins. Stylised: one rigid joint, noiseless, no friction.

projects.title: A continuous-time twin certifies PD at every gain: which gains survive a zero-order-hold sampled loop?
projects.summary: Double integrator under PD control computed at period T and held. The twin (T→0) is stable for every gain; the exact step matrix gives the real stable region kpT/2 < kd < 2/T, i.e. ωnT < min(4ζ, 1/ζ), matched to bisection and an independent RK4 held-input run (ζ=0.7 fails at ωnT=1.4286). The twin is accurate for ωnT ≲ 0.2 but at 1.2 the real overshoot is 0.234 against its 0.046, and at fixed T raising ωn past ωnT≈1 slows settling (0.4 → 5.2) then diverges. Deadbeat gains (kpT2=1, kdT=3/2) settle in 2 samples, the real speed limit. Stylised: noiseless, no computation delay.

projects.title: A linear-drag twin of a quadratic-drag vehicle: what does it get wrong about braking, terminal speed and the safe speed under a stopping limit?
projects.summary: Real drag cv|v|, twin kv with k matched at one speed. Coast-down time to fall to v0/10 is 9/(cv0) for the truth and independent of v0 in the twin (0.05×, 0.51×, 1.02× the truth at v0=1, 10, 20 for a fit at 5); terminal speed is off by vterm/vfit; a least-squares fit over [0, vmax] has k=3cvmax/4, exact only at 0.75vmax. The safe speed under a 10 m stopping limit is mis-stated by −20.8%, −8.9%, +7.0%, +41.1% for fits at 1, 5, 10, 20 m/s, so the error changes sign with the fit speed, and trace-fitted k falls from 0.382 to 0.223 as the coast-down lengthens because the slow tail dominates. Stylised: one dimension, pure quadratic drag, closed-form noiseless truth.

projects.title: A kinematic-bicycle twin ignores tyre slip: how wrong is its turning radius, and does calibrating that reveal where a twin-tuned steering loop goes unstable?
projects.summary: Real car: linear single-track model with tyre slip; twin: ψ′=vδ/L. Steering with the twin’s angle gives radius R(1+Kv2/L) for understeer gradient K, matched by simulation (R=100 m: 104.6, 118.5, 174.0, 266.4 m at 5, 10, 20, 30 m/s; twin 4–63% too small, exactly half at the characteristic speed 23.26 m/s; oversteer car up to 136% too large at 20 m/s). Fitting K removes that error exactly, yet both the kinematic and the calibrated twin certify δ=−kpy−kdψ as stable at every speed and gain, while 11 of a 30-point gain grid lose stability on the real car below 60 m/s (kp=0.4, kd=0.5: 14.0 m/s; confirmed in the time domain, 1.1×10−9 m at 8 m/s vs 4.6×107 m at 20 m/s). An oversteer car with feedback loses stability at 23.7 m/s, below its open-loop critical speed 26.33 m/s. Stylised: linear tyres, constant speed, no actuator lag or delay; the closed-loop limit is not derived in closed form.

projects.title: A grid twin over-states every route by a heading-dependent factor: does a finer grid fix it, and can it rank two routes the wrong way round?
projects.summary: Real route: a straight line of length L; twin: shortest path on a k-connected lattice. The grid/Euclid ratio depends on heading and connectivity, not cell size: 8-connected it is cosφ+(√2−1)sinφ, mean 8(√2−1)/π=1.0548 and worst 1.0824 at 22.5° (4-connected mean 1.2732, worst 1.4142; 16-connected 1.0144, 1.0275), matched by Dijkstra; refining the cell from 8 m to 0.1 m leaves a 100 m route at 22.5° at 1.0824. Calibrating by the mean leaves −5.2% to +2.6% (8-connected). For two routes of Euclidean length 1 and 1.03 at random headings the twin ranks the longer one shorter with probability 0.194 (0 at ratio ≥ 1.0824), and for a fixed pair 22.5° apart rotating the map flips the ranking for 31% of orientations. Stylised: free space only, no obstacles, length as a proxy for time or energy.

projects.title: A global-shutter twin of a rolling-shutter camera ignores target motion: how biased is a twin-trained orientation estimate, and what does the same frame reveal?
projects.summary: Row r is exposed at t=rτ/H, so a moving rectangle is imaged sheared and stretched; closed-form edge normals match a row-by-row simulation. At 1000 px/s horizontal speed the vertical edges tilt 3.58° and the horizontal ones 0, so averaging the two edge families (what a global-shutter twin certifies) is biased 1.79°; 1000 px/s vertical speed makes the target 6.7% taller. One frame of a known-size rectangle identifies orientation and both velocities in closed form: with 0.25 px edge noise orientation error falls from 0.24–0.97° to 0.027° and speeds are recovered to 16 and 4.8 px/s, but vertical speed is very sensitive to the assumed size (a 5% height error moves it by about 800 px/s). Stylised: straight edges, constant velocity, known size, no real footage.

projects.title: A snapshot twin of a spinning lidar ignores that the platform moves during the sweep: how biased is the map, what does one scan reveal, and what do yaw and acceleration do?
projects.summary: Real sensor: 2-D lidar at 10 Hz firing each beam at a different time while the platform moves; twin: all beams at t = 0. At 10 m/s the front and back walls are placed 0.25 and 0.75 m short, so apparent room length is biased by exactly vτ/2 = 0.50 m while the width is exact, and deskewing with the true motion removes it. Parallel walls appear to converge by ≈ vτ/(2π)(1/d1+1/d2) (1.94° measured vs 2.05° first order), so a wall-angle estimator certified on the snapshot twin inherits a heading bias; inverting that angle recovers speed from a single scan to 0.13 m/s at 1 cm range noise (first-order bias −1.8%). Yaw scales bearings by exactly −κβ/(1+κ), and acceleration biases scan-to-scan odometry by exactly a tf in velocity, bounded and non-accumulating. Stylised: 2-D rectangular room, constant velocity or acceleration along one axis, known platform motion.

projects.title: A satellite-positioning twin with white range noise certifies an error radius the real receiver does not meet: how wrong is it once multipath is correlated, and does averaging fix it?
projects.summary: Real receiver: 2-D position and clock from n pseudoranges with multipath; twin: white noise σ only. For an evenly spread constellation HDOP is exactly √(4/n) (simulated to 0.3%) and collapses to 4.25 over a 90° arc; one biased satellite of size b moves the fix by exactly 2b/n toward that satellite, which no amount of averaging removes. With AR(1) multipath (ρ = 0.99) the twin predicts a 1/√T gain but the simulated error only falls from 1.58 to 0.80 m over 500 epochs (exact 0.80), and a 95% radius calibrated on single epochs covers 33% of fixes at T = 10 and 5% at T = 100 (exact 31% and 5%). A residual integrity test tuned to 1% false alarms on the twin alarms 21% of the time when multipath equals the noise (exact closed form), and the statistic rises by only b²(1−3/n) while the position bias is 2b/n. Stylised: 2-D, linearised, evenly spread or arc constellations, stationary AR(1) multipath.

projects.title: A point-mass twin of a rolling body ignores rotational inertia: how wrong are acceleration, slip and coast distance, and what does one calibration fix?
projects.summary: A frictionless point mass overstates down-ramp acceleration by exactly 1+k (k=I/mr2: 1.4, 1.5, 2.0 for sphere, disc, hoop), so a 2 m descent takes 0.90 s instead of 1.07–1.28 s; a stick/slip simulation matches the closed forms to 3×10−4 m/s2. The slip threshold μ* = k tanα/(1+k) is invisible to the twin, and a launch speed picked in the twin to coast 1 m carries a rolling body 40–100% farther. A gain fitted on one shape removes its own error but leaves −16% to +20% fall-time error on the others (pooled fit +6.7% to −10.7%), and the twin cannot rank the shapes. Stylised: planar incline, Coulomb friction, no rolling resistance or drag, no hardware data.

projects.title: A pinhole twin of a radially distorted camera mis-ranges the near field: how far off does a twin-trained braking policy stop, and does focal calibration fix it?
projects.summary: With Brown distortion xd=x(1+k1r2) and a camera at height h, the pinhole twin reads floor range off by exactly 1/(1+k1h2/R2): for k1=−0.3, h=0.5 m that is +15.4% at 0.75 m, +8.1% at 1 m and +0.5% at 4 m. A policy trained to stop at 1.0 m stops at 0.909 m (16.4 cm short at 0.75 m; the first-order formula understates this at large ρ). Least-squares focal calibration (s=1+3k1ρmax2/5) moves the error rather than removing it: near-field 8.1% → 3.2% but a new 4.4% far-field under-read, and a 4 m stop lands 17 cm long. One image of a known grid identifies k1 (RMS 0.001 at 0.002 normalised-pixel noise). Stylised: one distortion term, axis-column floor points, known grid pose, no real lens.

projects.title: An instantaneous-exposure twin of a finite-exposure camera certifies detection at every speed: what is the real speed limit, and what does a blur-matched filter buy back?
projects.summary: A bar of width w moving d = vT px during the exposure is imaged as an exact trapezoid (peak C·min(1, w/d), energy Cw conserved), matching a 2000-sub-exposure simulation to its quantisation. A single-pixel peak detector that the twin certifies at Pd = 1 everywhere loses power as soon as d > w (at w = 6, C/σ = 10: Pd 1.00 → 0.28 at d = 24), with speed limit d* = wC/(σz) (13.7 px). A box filter of length d collects all of Cw at noise cost √d, output Cw/(σ√d)·(1−w/4d), so the limit grows quadratically in SNR: 5–55× faster over 12 settings, but it needs the speed, and a filter tuned on the twin (length w) still drops to Pd 0.26 at d = 60. Stylised: 1-D, known location, constant velocity, white Gaussian noise, no real footage.

projects.title: A twin with an ideal magnetometer returns the true heading: how large is the hard-iron and soft-iron error, what does it do to a compass-held path, and how much of a turn does a swing calibration need?
