projects.summary: A hard-iron offset β (relative to the field B) gives a peak heading error of exactly asin(β/B) (11.5° at 0.20, 53.1° at 0.80); soft-iron axis scaling r gives asin(|1−r|/(1+r)) (6.4° at r = 0.8), unchanged by removing the offset. A compass-held 100 m square misses its start by 2Lβ/B (2, 6, 20, 60 m at 0.01–0.3) for every offset direction tried, while the ideal twin closes to 10−14 m; a straight leg stays within 1 m cross-track for only 10–50 m at β/B = 0.02–0.10. A circle-fit swing calibration over a full turn has offset error ≈ 2σ/√n (0.0040 at n = 100), growing ×1.8 at 180°, ×12 at 90° and ×45 at 60° of turn (median heading residual 0.18° → 2.2° → 10.7°). Stylised: level 2-D sensor, simulated data, no gyro fusion, no ellipse fit; the 2Lβ/B closure law is verified numerically, not proved beyond first order.

projects.title: A gyro twin calibrated on white noise hides the bias random walk: how wrong are its heading error, re-alignment interval and dead-reckoning budget, and does a single-point Allan fit help?
projects.summary: Real rate = white noise N plus a random-walking bias K; the twin keeps only N. Heading variance is N2t + K2t3/3, so the real/twin ratio is exactly 1 + (t/t*)2 with t* = √3N/K = 86.6 s (2.33 at 100 s, 134 at 1000 s), confirmed by Monte Carlo and a simulated Allan deviation (within 3% for short averaging times, noisy at 1000 s). Re-aligning to keep 2σ heading within 1° is needed every 416 s; the twin allows 10 000 s (24×), where the real error exceeds 1° with probability 0.986. An Allan fit at 1–10 s changes nothing; a fit at τ0 = 100 s is exact only there (variance ratio 2.3 at 1 s, 0.18 at 300 s) and one at 1000 s is 5.6× too conservative. For 2σ cross-track error within 1 m the twin reports 1.74× (1 m/s) and 1.25× (5 m/s) too much usable distance. Stylised: linear-Gaussian, one axis, parameters chosen by me, no aiding, no real IMU data.

projects.title: A zero-wind twin of a UAV out-and-back leg: does a tailwind repay the headwind, and what does a twin calibrated on one leg say about the return?
projects.summary: Real round-trip energy is (v4+1)/(v2−w2), so wind does not cancel: real/twin is exactly 1/(1−(w/v)2), 1.33× at w/v=0.5 and 5.3× at 0.9, the same for either sign, with no return at |w|≥v. The twin-optimal airspeed is 1 for every wind while the real optimum solves v2=w2+√(w4+1), so flying the twin's optimum costs 1.5%, 9.8%, 52% extra at w=0.4, 0.6, 0.8. A twin calibrated on one leg and assumed to see the same wind back is off by exactly +w/v (headwind leg) or −w/v (tailwind leg): ±33% at w=0.5, v=1.5, with a sign set by which leg was flown. Stylised: steady along-track wind, constant airspeed, two-term power law.

projects.title: A constant-gain twin of a motor holding a load certifies every load: what does thermal derating do to the real hold?
projects.summary: Holding a torque dissipates Ri2; heating lowers the torque constant, so the hold current rises and heats more. In scaled variables φ′=λ/(1−φ)2−φ the hold exists iff λ≤4/27 (fold at φ=1/3) while the twin says φ=λ at every load: the real temperature rise is 1.33× and 1.76× the twin’s at λ=0.10 and 0.14 (current 1.15×, 1.33×) and 2.25× at the fold; above it there is no hold and the torque constant collapses in finite time, ≈4π/(9√ε) thermal time constants near the fold (ratio 0.925 at ε=0.002, 0.994 at 10−5). Tests shorter than the thermal time constant cannot see it (0.1 time constants at λ=0.14: +1.4% current). Under a winding temperature limit the twin overstates holdable torque by 1/(1−φm) (1.11× at φm=0.1, 1.64× at 0.4); refitting a constant gain on a hot low-load run still under-predicts (−0.06 to −0.10) and keeps no fold; winding-resistance rise lowers the fold (0.148 to 0.113 at β/α=1). Companion to the windup and gravity twins. Stylised: one thermal node, linear derating, constant load.

projects.title: What does a twin whose sensor reads at any distance get wrong about a loop with a range-limited lidar or radar?
projects.summary: A twin with unlimited sensor range predicts geometric convergence; a real sensor reading clip(x, −R, R) caps the approach speed at kR. The exact step-count law matches simulation in 108/108 cases; for k=0.25 the twin says 49 steps from 1000R and the real loop takes 4021 (82×), an error linear in x0/R with slope 1/k. For a PI loop the twin's overshoot is neither a bound nor a lower bound: smaller at 2–5R, 4.1× larger at 1000R; conditional integration repairs overshoot but not settling time. Logs within range fit the gain exactly and cannot reveal R; from logs uniform on [−L, L] the fitted gain factor is 1.5q−0.5q3, q=R/L. Stylised: scalar noiseless loop, hard symmetric clip.

projects.title: One long twin run or many replications when every run starts in the wrong state?
projects.summary: Splitting a fixed budget of N twin draws into r replications, each started at an offset and with d draws deleted, gives iid replication means, but the warm-up bias does not shrink with r. For an AR(1) the MSE and the exact coverage of the Student-t interval are closed-form (0.921 vs 0.921 simulated at r=50): a single run minimises MSE, replication costs at most 1.07× at φ=0.9 but 2.2× at φ=0.99, and the nominal-95% interval covers 92% at the MSE-optimal deletion once replications are short (no deletion reaches 94% at 40 draws each). Single-run batch means were not worse in this model. Preliminary M/M/1 simulation: 30 short replications cover 5.8% of the time, and no setting tried reaches 95%. Stylised: Gaussian AR(1), one start offset, simulated “real” system.

projects.title: How biased is a short digital-twin run that starts from a default state?
projects.summary: A twin reset to an empty queue and averaged over n steps is biased toward that start. For AR(1) output the bias, variance and best warm-up deletion are exact (bias/sd 1.88 to 0.12 for n=20 to 2500 at φ=0.9). For the M/M/1 wait the summed empty-start bias is ρ/(1−ρ)3 (verified numerically against an exact series and coupled simulation), so it equals one standard deviation only at 23 jobs at ρ=0.9: at run lengths that give a valid interval it costs 1–3 coverage points. Short runs are different: 50 jobs from an empty start read 5.6 below the true mean wait of 9; starting at the mean reduces bias but not reliably RMSE; a noisy real-state start is unbiased with 3.6× the sd; MSER-5 truncation made bias and coverage worse here. Stylised (AR(1) and M/M/1, simulated “real” system).

projects.title: How far should a real-plant estimate be pulled toward its digital twin?
projects.summary: Shrinking a real estimate of d plant parameters toward the twin's prediction (James–Stein) has an exact risk d−(d−2)<sup>2</sup>E[1/(d−2+2K)], K~Poisson(λ/2): it never raises total error for d≥3, a perfect twin gives risk 2 at any d (saving 33% at d=3, 80% at d=10), and a twin as noisy as the data (λ/d=1) still saves 14–49% while using it alone saves nothing. At large d the twin is worth n+σ<sup>2</sup>/τ<sup>2</sup> real samples (exact values 0.72–0.998 of that at d=5–100). The guarantee is aggregate only: one badly mismatched parameter among d takes about d/4 noise variances of damage (measured 2.9 at d=10, 25.5 at d=100 against 1), and blocks of 5 cap that at 1.65 (d=30) while keeping 72% of the perfect-twin saving. Stylised: Gaussian noise, orthogonal design, no robot data.

projects.title: What does a twin that assumes the radar is aligned with the body get wrong about dead reckoning, and can loop-closure validation see it?
projects.summary: With a planar mount-yaw error e, radar ego-velocity dead reckoning is exactly the true path rotated by e: error 2 sin(e/2)·|displacement|, bounded by the path diameter and zero after any closed loop, so loop and out-and-back validations pass while a straight 157 m run is off by 27 m at 10°. A closed-form rotation fit recovers e with standard deviation σ/√Σ|pi|2 (matched by simulation, 95% coverage). Stylised: the result is planar; a pitched mount drifts vertically by exactly laps·2πR sin e despite perfect x-y closure.

projects.title: How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when certifying a policy?
projects.summary: A twin evaluated alone is biased however many rollouts you run (nominal 95% intervals cover the truth 0–0.4% of the time at a 12% bias, 20% gain error); used as a control variate it removes variance without bias. In scalar LQ the rollout cost is a Gaussian quadratic form, so the twin/plant correlation ρ = λ tr(GG′)/√(tr G2 tr G′2) is exact, the optimal twin-to-real ratio is ρ/√((1−ρ2)w) and the speed-up 1/(√(1−ρ2)+ρ√w)2, matched by simulation to a few percent. Twin gain error is first order in the bias (5% error → 2.7%) but second order in 1−ρ, so the twin’s value is capped by the fraction λ of the real disturbance it can replay: a 5% certificate costs 168 real-only, 28 with λ = 0.95 and 163 with λ = 0.3. Twin-only beats real-only only below σ2/bias2 real rollouts (35 at 10% error). Stylised.

projects.title: What does a Gaussian-clutter radar twin promise about detection, not just false alarms?
projects.summary: With CA- and OS-CFAR thresholds set in a Gaussian twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter, the exact false-alarm and detection laws (including a new one-dimensional OS-CFAR law) match simulation to ~1%. OS-CFAR is inflated much like CA (design 1e-4, ν=2: 30× vs 35×). Repairing the threshold costs 3.7–4.6 dB, yet the SNR needed for Pd = 0.9 at Pfa = 1e-4 is 6.3 dB above the twin’s promise at ν=2 (2.8 dB at ν=5, 0.8 dB at ν=20), and at the twin’s own threshold and promised SNR real Pd is 0.84 while Pfa is 30× design. Texture does not reverse the CA-beats-OS ranking (a negative result). Stylised: iid gamma texture, constant-SNR target, no interferers, no real radar data.

projects.title: How do you estimate a controller's real-world cost with a biased digital twin?
projects.summary: A twin-only cost estimate is biased by the twin’s error, a real-only one is noisy; as a control variate the twin keeps the estimate unbiased and is worth its correlation with real rollouts, not its accuracy. Under common disturbances the cost correlation has a closed form and decays as (1+c4)/(1−c4)2(kδ)2 in the twin’s gain error (0.985, 0.941, 0.782, 0.472 for gains 1.15, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0 while the twin-only bias grows 0.004 to 1.34); replaying only a fraction λ of the real disturbance multiplies it by exactly λ2. The optimal twin-to-real rollout ratio is √(crρ2/(ct(1−ρ2))), the twin pays only below price (1−√(1−ρ2))2/ρ2, and a simulated estimator cut variance to 0.228 of real-only against 0.225 predicted. Twin-only wins at tiny budgets or tiny bias; the control variate is best elsewhere. Stylised.

projects.title: How fast can a deployed digital twin be caught going stale, and when is it invisible?
projects.summary: An e-process on the twin's closed-loop prediction residuals is valid however often it is checked (2.3% false alarms versus 51.6% for a repeatedly refit χ2 test at nominal 5%). Its detection rate is exactly the twin-transfer score gap, affine in the exploration variance v; a mixture-delay formula matches simulated medians within 10–20% (leading order L/rate is 40–55% too fast). Twins on the line Δa = kΔb are invisible under the deployed policy (rate exactly 0) and detectable at rate Δb2v/2σ2 with dither; most of them cost almost nothing (regret 6·10−4) so dither does not pay, but the one that thinks the actuator is nearly dead (regret 0.23) is worth a v≈0.006 dither that cuts expected cost 12×. Stylised.

projects.title: How far can DiLoCo reports be compressed?
projects.summary: Unbiased compression of each worker’s pseudo-gradient (noise proportional to the signal, ω) has exact stationary variance αVw(1+ω)/(Ms(2−αsc)), c = 1+ω/M: it caps the outer step at 2/(sc) and the contraction at 1−1/c (keeping 10% of coordinates with 8 workers: 0.53, 22 rounds to 10−6 against 1), and random participation is the special case ω = 1/p−1. Dithered quantisation only adds Δ2/12 to the variance and leaves stability alone. At fixed bandwidth, sparsifying favours few full reports, while quantising has an interior optimum near 1.3 bits per coordinate with many workers, about 4× below 8-bit reports (the textbook high-resolution law understates the noise 2.9× at 1 bit). Matched to simulation within 3%. Stylised.

projects.title: What does it cost to send only a fraction of the outer update, and does error feedback help?
projects.summary: Each worker transmits a random fraction p of its pseudo-gradient. Rescaling the subset (unbiased) inflates the stationary noise floor by exactly 1/p. Adding a per-worker error-feedback memory gives an exact closed form from a four-dimensional second-moment recursion and costs only 1 + αs(1/p − 1) at small steps, for any number of workers, because the virtual iterate follows uncompressed SGD. The price is speed: the mean dynamics have determinant 1 − p, so the contraction cannot beat √(1 − p) per round; over a 400-round horizon error feedback reaches 0.39, 0.24 and 0.17 of the unbiased loss at p = 0.25, 0.1, 0.03, and the advantage disappears when the horizon is shorter than about 1/p. Stylised: diagonal quadratics, Bernoulli masks, no top-k.

projects.title: Can a DiLoCo-style run hide its synchronisation by applying the outer update rounds late?
projects.summary: Applying the outer step τ rounds late gives a mode the recursion xt+1 = xt − αs xt−τ, stable iff αs < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1). The best step sits at that edge, so the rate is 1 − 2 sin(π/(4τ+2))/κH (exactly κH/(κH+1) at τ=1), and outer momentum stops helping the moment τ ≥ 1 (69 rounds at τ=0 become 1388 at κH=100). Even with the sync fully hidden the gain over blocking averaging is at most (τ+1) sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≤ 1, and an exact search over (H, τ) finds overlapped training 1.5–4.9× slower than blocking averaging and 2.3–31× slower than blocking with tuned momentum. Giving the fresh pseudo-gradient weight above ½ removes the penalty entirely (stable for every τ; at weight 0.75 and τ=1 the stale term acts as negative momentum, 2× faster than no delay). Stylised: noiseless quadratic, shared Hessian, one common delay.

projects.title: A twin whose wind gusts are matched to the logged variance each step: how wrong is the position variance of a PD-held vehicle, and does matching the spectrum instead fix it?
projects.summary: Real gust: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck with rate a and variance s2; exact real variance s2(a+kd)/(kdkp(a2+akd+kp)). A twin drawing iid gusts per step has variance s2dt/(2kdkp): 141× too small at a=1, dt=0.01 (270× at a=0.05), a standard deviation scaling as √dt, and a 10−3 margin that the real system exceeds 78% of the time. A spectrum-matched white twin is always conservative, real/twin = a(a+kd)/(a2+akd+kp) < 1 (0.71 at a=1). Fitting the OU rate from logged wind recovers the real variance (within 1% at 105 samples). Stylised: linear loop, Gaussian gusts, no wind data.

projects.title: A free-space radar twin ignores ground-bounce lobing: how wrong is it, and can a two-ray twin with a slightly wrong target height be worse?
projects.summary: Two-ray detection 16 sin4u, u=2πhrht/(λr): lobe-mean gain exactly 6 and a detected phase fraction 1−(2/π)asin((c/16)1/4), exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge. The real system misses 20% of ranges inside the free-space range and detects 44% of those beyond it. A deterministic two-ray twin with height error δh disagrees ≈4hrδh/(λr) (0.200 at 0.5 m, matching simulation) and is worse than free space at short range; a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 against 0.197 deterministic and 0.533 free space. Stylised: perfect reflection, flat earth, hard threshold, no radar data.

projects.title: A point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers: it has the right median, so what does it get wrong, and does averaging looks converge where it says?
projects.summary: Ideal monopulse on two unresolved scatterers (strong 1, weak r, random phase) gives Y=(1−r2)/(1+r2+2rcosφ): the mean is exactly the strong scatterer and the median exactly the power centroid, variance 2r2/(1−r2), and the estimate lies outside the target span with probability arccos(r)/π. A variance-matched Gaussian centroid twin gets the median right and the mean wrong by 2r2/(1+r2), is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate at r=0.9, and predicts √(var/N) for averaged looks where the real mean floors at that bias (0.90 vs 0.09 at N=1024); the median converges and beats the mean on variance for r≥0.477. Stylised: noise-free ideal monopulse, two scatterers, no radar data.

projects.title: A constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: which dark/bright decision rule does it teach, and what does that cost on the real sensor?
projects.summary: For Poisson counts the Bayes dark/bright threshold is the logarithmic mean (λ<sub>1</sub>−λ<sub>0</sub>)/ln(λ<sub>1</sub>/λ<sub>0</sub>); a Gaussian twin with one matched variance puts it at the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), and a square-root twin lands in between at (A+G)/2. A detector tuned in the arithmetic twin has 1.25× the optimal real error at (4,12), 1.83× at (10,30) and 1.74× at (50,100), and with λ<sub>1</sub>=2λ<sub>0</sub> the penalty grows to 23× at λ<sub>0</sub>=200, while the twin’s own predicted error stays within 1.8× of the optimum; the square-root rule recovers the optimal integer rule in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised: ideal Poisson counts, no read noise, no camera data.

projects.title: A radar twin whose targets occupy a single range cell: how far around a strong target does the real matched filter ghost, and does tapering fix it?
projects.summary: A lone strong target through a matched filter alarms at neighbouring cells with an exact Rician probability where the point-response twin says Pfa0=10−6: at the rect peak sidelobe (−13.3 dB) it is 0.020 at 20 dB SNR and 1.0 at 30 dB, and the ghost zone radius grows √10 per 10 dB (3 to 331 cells for 20–60 dB). Tapers raise the ghost-free SNR by exactly the sidelobe-level difference plus the ENBW loss (20.0 dB Hann, 30.8 dB Hamming) at 1.5–1.6× mainlobe width, but ordering by peak sidelobe misleads at very strong targets: Hamming’s 1/x far sidelobes give a 42-cell zone against Hann’s 7 at 60 dB. A weak target beside a 40 dB one is ‘detected’ with Pd=1.0 where the empty cell alarms with probability 1.0. Stylised: white output noise, no CFAR or clutter, no radar data.

projects.title: A link twin with independent packet loss says to send repeats back to back: what does burstiness do to repetition coding for shared maps, and what does spacing buy?
projects.summary: An update is sent as r copies g slots apart and is lost only if all are. Against a two-state loss chain with the same marginal rate p = 0.2 and lag-1 correlation λ, the exact residual is p(p + λg(1−p))r−1 against the twin’s pr. The twin’s 5 back-to-back copies for 10−3 give a real residual of 0.026 at λ = 0.5 and 0.10 at 0.8 (81× and 311× the claim); two copies need spacing of 6 to 36 slots to come within 10% of the twin. With at most 8 copies the minimum-latency design is 12 to 154 slots (λ = 0.5 to 0.95) against the twin’s 4, and with at most 4 copies no spacing reaches 10−3. A counter-case: with no copy budget and a long deadline, back-to-back copies still beat a few spaced ones. Stylised: simulated link, known stationary parameters, no radio traces.

projects.title: A lidar twin without atmospheric loss overstates range in fog: by how much, how sensitive is it to a mis-set extinction, and what does it do to a driving policy?
projects.summary: Detection range solves reαr = r0, i.e. r = W(αr0)/α; the clear-air twin overstates it by exactly eαr (×2.32 at 200 m visibility) and a relative extinction error moves range by the elasticity W/(1+W) < 1. With lognormal episode-to-episode fog a policy sized on the median fog is violated 50% of the time (mean fog 34%), the 5%-quantile range gives exactly 5% at a 43.5% speed cost, and in patchy fog one extinction calibrated on a bright target underestimates dark targets by up to 29% (calibrated on a dark one, bright targets are overestimated 61–168%). Stylised: hard threshold, Beer–Lambert medium, no lidar data.

projects.title: Is a clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin right when rain comes in cells?
projects.summary: Radar detection range under intermittent rain attenuation. The power law in rain rate has a Jensen gap (1.52× the mean-rate attenuation), so a mean-rate twin (closed-form Lambert W range, 18.84 km) is reached by only 39% of real storm fields; matching the mean attenuation barely helps (Brier 0.054 vs 0.055). A rain ensemble scores 0.038 vs 0.101 for clear air, and long cells flip the mean-rate twin from optimistic to pessimistic. Stylised: simulated rain, illustrative coefficients, no radar data.

projects.title: How long must a real test run be when its length was sized in a twin with the wrong plant pole?
projects.summary: A gain designed in a twin whose pole is m× the real one is validated on hardware for a run length chosen in the twin. The variance of the time-averaged cost of a Gaussian AR(1) loop is exact and depends on the closed-loop pole through (1+ρ)/(1−ρ), ρ=ac2, so the twin-sized run is 3.8× too short at m=2, r=0.1 (3,177 vs 12,110 steps; real coverage of a ±5% claim 0.69 vs 0.95 nominal, simulated 0.68) and 2.1× too long at m=1.5, r=5; an oscillating (negative-pole) loop averages as slowly as a sluggish one. Sizing from a real pilot’s lag-one autocorrelation is close to median-unbiased but under-sizes about half the time. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, fixed known gain, normal-approximation interval.

projects.title: What does a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certify?
projects.summary: A pulsed Doppler radar reports radial velocity modulo 2V; a twin that renders velocity as a real number never aliases. The real bias of a wrapped return is an exact Gaussian tail series (−V at speed V, −2V beyond) and the real MSE has a bias2 floor, so averaging widens the gap to the twin's claim s2/n: at V=10, s=1 and speed 8 the real/claimed MSE is 7.9× for one return and 2.1×103 for 104. Speeds with |bias| ≤ 0.1 reach only 87%, 74% and 48% of V for noise 0.5, 1, 2. Unwrapping against a prior has exact failure probability 2Φ(−V/√(s2+sp2)) and stays within 10% of the twin's claim only for prior error ≤ 0.26V. Stylised: one radial channel, Gaussian noise, simulated radar.

projects.title: Which rungs of a ladder of digital twins are worth running?
projects.summary: For twins of decreasing cost and fidelity used as nested control variates the variance is exact, σ<sup>2</sup>Σ(ρ<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>−ρ<sub>i+1</sub><sup>2</sup>)/m<sub>i</sub>, and a cheaper rung pays below a twin already in use iff ρ<sub>2</sub>/ρ<sub>1</sub> > 2√r/(1+r) (0.943 for halved cost, 0.575 for a 10× drop), the single-twin threshold applied to the step correlation. Using every rung is not best (q=0.99, r=0.5, six rungs: 0.284 of real-only variance vs 0.196 for the best two; q=0.9 makes all rungs 1.41× worse than real-only while the best subset gets 0.83), and 10 of 336 paying grid points are infeasible. On a saturated PD mass-spring timestep ladder the best ladder reaches 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 for the best single twin), collapsing to the cheapest twin at 90%/70% disturbance replay (0.52/0.89 simulated); a coarser rung diverged in 2 of 20,000 contexts. Stylised: one plant, known correlations, step-count costs.

projects.title: A heartbeat twin that drops packets independently: how often does the real bursty link trip a missed-beat watchdog, and what timeout is safe?
projects.summary: At 5% mean loss a watchdog that e-stops after m = 5 missed heartbeats false-trips once in 3.4×106 ticks (18.7 h at 50 Hz) in the i.i.d.-loss twin but every 235–990 ticks (5–20 s) on a two-state bursty link with mean burst 2–50, from an exact recursion checked against enumeration and Monte Carlo. The error is not monotone in burst length: it is worst at L ≈ m, where the mean time to trip is only ≈ em/p. For a 106-tick target the twin picks m = 5 (0.10 s to detect a dead link) while the real link needs 16–154 (0.3–3.1 s) growing linearly in L, and with L unknown no affordable timeout guarantees it. Stylised: Gilbert channel, plain miss counter, no link traces.

projects.title: A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: does an innovation gate help or hurt the real estimator, and what does it do after a jump?
projects.summary: With a Gaussian-sensor twin an innovation gate (z = 2.58) costs 8.5% of the update MSE, since every gated measurement is good data; with 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the same gate cuts the MSE 1.74 → 0.58 (3.0×) while still passing 28% of the outliers. The ungated error grows like κ2 in the outlier scale, the gated error is bounded and worst at a finite κ* ≈ 4, and a better-tuned gate width gains only 0–6%. After a jump D in a random-walk state the gate rejects the correct measurements and re-convergence takes ≈ 76D2 steps (30,512 at D = 20) against 30 with no gate. Exact post-update MSE checked by quadrature and Monte Carlo. Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, simplified covariance rule in the jump experiment.

projects.title: What does a linear photon-counter twin of a SPAD lidar miss about dead time?
projects.summary: An ideal counter twin reads flux linearly; a real detector with dead time τ reports half the flux at nτ=1 (non-paralyzable) or 36.8% (paralyzable), and the paralyzable curve peaks at 1/e, so one reading has two fluxes (0.259 or 2.543 at mτ=0.2; a twin is 12.7× too low on the high branch). First-photon timing of a Gaussian pulse is biased early by −N/(2√π)σ at small N (exact) and saturating near −2σ: −0.28σ at N=1 and −1.50σ at N=10 (−22.6 cm for σ=1 ns) while the spread shrinks to 0.62σ, so it is bias, not averaging noise. A Coates correction of the first-photon histogram restores the mean to within 0.02σ. Stylised: one pulse, no background light, afterpulsing or crosstalk.

projects.title: What ghost ranges does a single-ray lidar twin never produce at a depth edge?
projects.summary: A one-ray twin returns the near or the far surface at a depth edge; a real beam with a Gaussian footprint and merged return pulses reports an energy-weighted range in free space. The ghost band is exactly 2Φ−1(1−ε/D) beam standard deviations wide for equal energies (2.56 at ε/D = 0.1, 4.65 at 0.01, none once ε ≥ D/2), checked against a direct scan to 10−4, and shifts toward the near side and narrows when the far wall is brighter (1.67 at a 100× energy ratio). A scan with an edge every ≈ 100 beams has a ghost fraction equal to the prediction to within 0.3%, and a 3-of-5 persistence filter on a static robot passes 80–99% of ghosts because they come from geometry, not noise. Stylised: hard merge threshold, 1-D footprint, centroid detector, no real scans.

projects.title: What does an FMCW radar twin without range–Doppler coupling get wrong about a moving target?
projects.summary: A sawtooth chirp radar reads a moving target’s range as R + κv, κ = fcT/B; the twin reads R. A signal-level beat-tone simulation matches the formula to ≤ 10−4 range cells, and the bias is fDT cells independent of bandwidth: 0.6, 3.1 and 4.8 cells (9 cm, 46 cm, 2.9 m) at 30 m/s for fast 77 GHz, mid 77 GHz and slow 24 GHz ramps. Within the unambiguous speed it is under half a cell, but compensating with the radar’s own wrapped Doppler is worse than doing nothing on exactly half of the over-range speeds. For a stationary scene (±60°) a centroid fit absorbs 0.71κv of along-track position error and leaves 0.46κv rms distortion. Stylised: single up ramp, noise-free tone, no radar data.

projects.title: Does a well-featured twin overstate scan-matching accuracy in a corridor, where the scan cannot see the along-track direction?
projects.summary: In a bare corridor the point-to-line information matrix is exactly singular along the track and the matcher returns its initial guess; door-frame stubs every 20/10/5/2 m give an exact along-track sd of 8.1/6.3/3.9/2.2 mm (MC 7.3/6.2/4.3/2.4), 1.6–6× a well-featured room's 1.35 mm, while lateral accuracy (≈ 0.8 mm) is unchanged. A Kalman filter fed the room twin's 1.9 mm covariance across a 20 m blind span has NEES 432 (1 cm/step odometry) and 1535 (2 cm/step) against 0.75 for the exact-covariance filter; the exact covariance is valid only inside a matcher basin of ≈ 0.2 m, and the covariance-aware filter is still overconfident at re-entry (NEES 2–8). Stylised: simulated 2D lidar, one-dimensional filter.

projects.title: A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: how many particles does a bootstrap filter need, and is the average effective sample size the right thing to size on?
projects.summary: For a bootstrap particle filter the large-N effective-sample-size fraction is exactly c0 e−ay² in the measurement y (c0 = 0.866, a = 1/6 at P = R = 1). With 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the mean ESS fraction barely moves (0.671 in the twin, 0.645 real, at every dimension), but P(ESS < 1% of N) goes from 2.5×10−4 to 3.1×10−2 (120×). Sizing N = 528 for ESS ≥ 50 at 1% failure in the twin fails 4.4% of real steps, and the particle posterior mean's error against the exact Kalman update is 45× to 421× the twin's for N = 50 to 1000, falling barely at all with N. The large-N formula is checked against quadrature and simulation and fails once Nρ is small (reported). Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, no resampling dynamics.
